intro:
**The Standard of Discrimination and the Servants of the Merciful**

Al-Furqān, "The Criterion," is the twenty-fifth chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 77 verses of mature Makkan revelation. It takes its name from the profound opening verse: *“Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (*al-Furqān*) upon His servant that he may be to the worlds a warner”* (25:1). *Al-Furqān* is one of the most significant titles of the sacred scripture, derived from the Arabic root *f-r-q*, signifying that which cuts, divides, and decisively discriminates between truth and falsehood, light and darkness, justice and tyranny, and authentic worship and hollow superstition. Positioned as the majestic portal to the mid-Makkan theological discourse, Sūrah al-Furqān addresses the cynical intellectual objections raised by the pagan elite against the human nature of the Prophet and the oral descent of scripture, culminating in one of the most breathtaking moral descriptions in all of world literature: the portrait of the *ʿIbād al-Raḥmān* (The Servants of the Most Compassionate) in verses 63–77.

**The Structural Symphony of the Criterion**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Furqān unfolds across three magnificent movements. The opening movement (1–34) exalts the unshared sovereignty of God Who has taken no son and has no partner in dominion, refutes the pagan claim that the Qur'an is an ancient fable dictated by others, and portrays the terrifying regret of the oppressor on the Day of Judgment: biting his own hands in despair and crying: *“Oh, I wish I had taken with the Messenger a way! Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that person as an intimate friend! He led me astray from the message after it had come to me”* (25:27–29). It records the poignant complaint of the Messenger on that Day: *“O my Lord, indeed my people took this Qur'an as a thing abandoned (*mahjūrā*)”* (25:30). The second movement (35–62) reviews the tragic historical fate of past civilizations who treated truth as a joke: the people of Moses, the people of Noah drowned in the flood, the giants of ʿĀd and Thamūd, the dwellers of al-Rass, and the ruined cities of Sodom showered with stones. It presents cosmic signs: the elongation of the shadow, the night as a garment, sleep as rest, winds carrying good tidings before rain, and the miraculous oceanic barrier: two seas meeting side by side—one fresh and sweet, the other salty and bitter—separated by an impassable barrier (*barzakh*) and a partition that cannot be breached (25:53). The third movement (63–77) forms the radiant moral climax of the sūrah, detailing the twelve virtues of the *ʿIbād al-Raḥmān* (Servants of the Merciful): those who walk upon the earth with humility; who, when addressed by the ignorant, reply gently with words of peace (*qālū salāmā*); who spend the night prostrating and standing before their Lord; who beg for deliverance from the punishment of Hell; who are neither extravagant nor tight-fisted in spending, maintaining a noble balance; who never invoke partners with God, murder, or commit adultery; who never bear false witness; and who pray the immortal family prayer: *“Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes and make us a leader for the righteous”* (25:74). The sūrah concludes (77) by stripping away human self-importance: *“Say, 'My Lord would not care for you were it not for your prayer/supplication!'”*

They scoffed: *“What is this messenger that eats food and walks through the marketplaces? Why was there not sent down to him an angel to be a warner with him? Or why is not a treasure dropped down to him, or why does he not have a garden from which he may eat?”* (25:7–8).

verses.1:
> Blessed is the One Who sent down the Standard to His servant, so that he may be a warner to the whole world

**The Opening Word as a Claim About Its Speaker**

The sūrah opens with *tabāraka*, a word whose Arabic root carries the meaning of continuous growth and increase in goodness (from *barakah*, blessing). Applied to God, it does not suggest that He changes or grows — a concern that moved some exegetes to prefer "holy" or "transcendent" as a translation — but declares that the source of all blessing is Himself, eternally and without interruption. The opening is not a greeting or an invocation; it is an assertion about the character of the One who acts. Everything that follows in the sūrah — the sending down, the warning, the rejection, the punishment, the reward — flows from a speaker whose nature is *tabāraka*. The word places the entire chapter under a theological claim: the revelation that arrives is not an afterthought but an expression of a generosity that precedes creation.

The structure mirrors other Qur'anic doxologies. Sūrah 67 opens with *tabāraka'lladhī bi-yadihi'l-mulk* — "Blessed is He in Whose hand is all sovereignty" (67:1). Sūrah 23:68 asks, "Have they not reflected on the Word, or has there come to them what did not come to their fathers of old?" The doxology in 25:1 answers that question by placing the Word inside a declaration of divine praise before any argument begins. The placement is architecturally significant: every objection the disbelievers raise in the chapters that follows — that the messenger eats food (25:7), that the revelation is fabricated (25:4), that it should have come all at once (25:32) — stands against a speaker who has already been named as the source of all blessing. The doxology is not decoration; it is the frame inside which every subsequent argument operates.

**Al-Furqān: The Criterion That Separates**

The title word *al-Furqān* comes from the root *f-r-q*, meaning to separate or divide. In the Qur'an it names both the Torah given to Moses (2:53; 21:48) and the revelation given to Muhammad ﷺ, functioning as a standard by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, the lawful from the prohibited, and the guided from the lost. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, in his *Mufradāt*, defines it as that which separates truth from falsehood, emphasizing its role as a moral and judicial instrument rather than merely a literary text.

Some modern scholars, drawing on pre-Islamic Arabic poetry and the work of the lexicographer al-Azharī (10th century), have proposed that *furqān* also carried the meaning of "dawn" — the moment when light separates from darkness. Whether or not this semantic layer was present in the audience's ear, the dominant Qur'anic usage is the one the sūrah exploits: a thing that cuts a line between two states that would otherwise blur. The word appears elsewhere with this force in 2:177, where the Book functions as a criterion within a larger list of beliefs and obligations, and in 8:29 and 8:41, where the *furqān* is given to those who believe and distinguish right from wrong. The Criterion is not a passive text; it is an active instrument that judges its reader as much as the reader judges it. The verse says "His servant" (*'abdihi*) without naming Muhammad ﷺ, a feature shared with 17:1 — "Glory be to the One Who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque." The title *'abd* (servant) is the highest honorific the Qur'an assigns to the Prophet. It appears at moments of supreme significance — the night journey, the opening of this sūrah, and the final commissioning in 33:56.

This is not to diminish the uniqueness of prophethood — the sūrah will make clear that no messenger before him was different in kind (25:20) — but to establish that the Standard requires a human carrier, and the carrier's humanity is not a deficiency in the message.

Compare 21:107, "We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds," where the same word *'ālamīn* carries the same universal charge but the operative noun is mercy, not warning.
verses.2:
> ˹Allah is˺ the One to Whom belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, Who has never had ˹any˺ offspring, nor does He have a partner in ˹governing˺ the kingdom. He has created everything, ordaining it precisely

**Taqdīr: Ordaining With Precise Measure**

The phrase *wa qaddarahu taqdīrā* — "and He has created everything, ordaining it precisely" — uses a verb (*qaddara*) and its cognate noun (*taqdīr*) together, a construction the Qur'an employs for emphasis. The root carries two interlocking meanings: to know the measure of a thing, and to assign a measure to it. God does not merely create and then estimate; He creates by measuring, and the measurement is the creation's defining feature. Al-Rāzī distinguishes between human *taqdīr*, which is assessment after the fact, and divine *taqdīr*, which is determination before the fact — God's knowledge of a creature's entire existence, from origin to end, is itself the act of ordainment.

This has direct consequences for the theological debate over *qadar* (predestination). The verse does not settle the question of how human freedom relates to divine decree — later theology will spend centuries on that — but it does establish the premise: nothing in creation is unmeasured. Every creature, every event, every limit is set by the One who owns the kingdom. The commentators who emphasize *taqdīr* as ordainment point to verses like 54:49 — "Indeed, all things We created with *qadar*" — and 65:3 — "He will provide for him from where he does not expect." The measuring is comprehensive; it includes the provision, the term, and the outcome. The parallel in 76:16 — "reclining on couches lined with silk brocade, and the fruit of both gardens is near at hand" — uses the same root in a different context to describe the precision of Paradise's provisions, showing that *taqdīr* applies not only to creation but to reward.

**A Denial That Closes Every Exit**

This is not a philosophical treatise compressed into a line; it is a practical argument addressed to people who have "taken gods apart from Him" (25:3). Every denial in 25:2 is the ground for the indictment in 25:3. If God has no offspring and no partner, then the false gods are neither His children nor His delegates. If everything is precisely measured, then the false gods have no independent power to create, sustain, or destroy. The theology of 25:2 is not abstract; it is the prosecution's opening statement, and 25:3 will present the evidence.

**Cross-Referencing Sovereignty Across the Qur'an**

The declaration that the kingdom belongs to God alone recurs across the Qur'an in contexts that sharpen its force. In 3:189 — "To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah has power over all things" — the statement follows a description of the Day when every soul will find what it has done presented before it. Sovereignty there is the framework for accountability: the Owner of all things judges all things. In 36:83 — "So glory be to the One in Whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will all be returned" — the word *subḥān* (glory) appears, and the return is specified. The same structure appears in 25:2: the One who owns everything has created everything with measure, and to that measured creation the disbelievers will return.
verses.3:
> Yet they have taken besides Him gods who cannot create anything but are themselves created. Nor can they protect or benefit themselves. Nor can they control life, death, or resurrection

**The Qur'an's Persistent Argument Against Idol Incompetence**

This verse does not stand alone; it belongs to a sustained Qur'anic argument that appears across multiple sūrahs with varying emphases. In 7:191 — "Do they associate with Him those who create nothing and are themselves created?" — the same first charge is stated as a question, forcing the audience to answer it themselves. In 16:20 — "Those they invoke besides Allah do not create anything; rather, they are themselves created" — the statement is even more compressed. The charge about inability to harm or benefit appears in 5:76, 10:18, 10:106, 13:16, and 21:66, each time in a slightly different argumentative context.

The Qur'an adds additional charges in other passages: idols cannot grant provision (16:73; 29:17), they cannot speak (78:37), and they cannot intercede on the Day of Judgment (30:13; 39:43; 43:86). Each new passage places the indictment in a fresh argument. Here, in 25:3, the charges follow the assertion of God's sole sovereignty and precise creation in 25:2. The argument is structural: the One who owns everything and measures everything has no need of, and no room for, a partner who owns nothing and measures nothing. The worshippers are not only wrong; they are inconsistent with their own theology. If they believe God created everything with measure (25:2), they cannot logically worship what cannot create at all (25:3).

**The Widening Scope: From Idols to All False Dependencies**

The word *yamlikūn* (they have, control) in the final clause is particularly sharp. The same root (*m-l-k*) appeared in 25:2 to describe God's sovereignty. The linguistic echo between the two verses — *mulk* in 25:2, *yamlikūn* in 25:3 — tightens the argument further: the One who owns the kingdom is contrasted with what owns nothing.

**The Body Speaks: When Idols Are Given a Voice**

One of the most striking features of the Qur'anic treatment of false worship is the scene, described elsewhere, in which the idols themselves testify against their worshippers. In 36:65 — "That Day, We will seal their mouths. Their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will testify to what they used to earn" — the human body is given voice; in the parallel scene involving the idols, the objects of worship are made to deny that they were ever worshipped at all. This will appear later in this very sūrah at 25:17-19, where God gathers the false deities and asks whether they misled His servants. The idols' answer, as recorded there, echoes the logic of 25:3: "Glory be to You! It was not right for us to take any lords besides You.".

The incapacity described in 25:3 — they cannot create, cannot sustain, cannot govern — is precisely what the idols will confess when given the chance to speak. The charge made here in Mecca is the testimony they will give on the Day of Judgment. The effect is one of prophetic irony: the Qur'an pronounces the verdict before the trial, and the verdict will be confirmed by the defendants themselves. The false gods will say, on the Day when speech is granted to all things, exactly what this verse says about them now.
verses.4:
> The disbelievers say, “This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but a fabrication which he made up with the help of others.” Their claim is totally unjustified and untrue

**Ifk: The Qur'an's Strongest Word for Falsehood**

The word *ifk* is one of the harshest terms the Qur'an uses for a lie. It appears in the context of the slander against Mary (19:27), and in the accusation against Joseph's master's wife (12:24, 12:28). In every case, *ifk* names not a honest mistake but a deliberate inversion of truth — calling good evil, calling revelation fabrication, calling chastity adultery. The disbelievers' use of this word against the Quran is itself an act of *ifk*: they take the most consequential truth claim of their time and label it the most consequential lie.

**The Charge That Returns in Every Generation**

The accusation in 25:4 is not unique to seventh-century Makkah; it is the standard objection to any claim of revelation. The same charge was leveled against Moses in Pharaoh's court: "This is indeed a well-contrived sorcery" (10:76). The same charge appears in the description of those who say of the Quran, "This is nothing but the word of a mortal" (74:25). The sūrah's placement of this accusation at the very beginning — after the doxology (25:1) and the theology of sovereignty (25:2-3) — tells the reader what the chapter is about. This is not a historical report of an old argument; it is the argument the sūrah exists to answer.

The disbelievers' approach reveals a method. They do not engage the content of the Quran; they question its origin. This is the structure of every dismissal that avoids the text: rather than refute what the Quran says, they explain where it came from. The sūrah will respond to this strategy in multiple ways — by pointing to the Quran's own internal coherence (25:33), by asking why the disbelievers cannot produce something like it if it is human, and by describing the consequences of the rejection in vivid Last-Day terms (25:11-16). But the response begins here, with a simple declaration: the accusation is *ẓulm* and *zūr*. Before any argument is offered, the claim is named for what it is.

**Why the Verse Does Not Argue Further**

A notable feature of 25:4 is its brevity. It records the accusation and pronounces it unjust and crooked, but it does not mount a defense. The defense comes in the verses that follow: the revelation comes from the Knower of all secrets (25:6), the Prophet is not unique in being human (25:20), and the Quran was sent in stages deliberately (25:32). The rhetorical strategy is important. The accusation is given its own verse — space, weight, and dignity — and then it is answered point by point across the rest of the sūrah. The effect is that the reader encounters the full force of the objection before hearing the reply, and the reply, when it comes, addresses the objection from every angle rather than from one. This is not evasion; it is architecture. The sūrah trusts its reader to hold the accusation in mind while the answer unfolds, and the answer is stronger for the delay. The accusation stands; the defense will follow; and the defense will outlast the accusation because it addresses not one charge but all of them.
verses.5:
> And they say, “˹These revelations are only˺ ancient fables which he has had written down, and they are rehearsed to him morning and evening.”

**The Second Accusation: Borrowed Tales**

Where 25:4 charged the Prophet ﷺ with fabricating the Quran with human help, 25:5 advances a different theory: the material was not invented but copied from older written sources. The phrase *asāṭīru'l-awwalīn* — "ancient fables" or "tales of the ancients" — recurs across the Qur'an (6:25; 8:31; 16:24; 23:83; 27:68; 46:17; 68:15; 83:13), each time as a label the disbelievers apply to the narratives the Quran contains: stories of earlier prophets, earlier nations, earlier punishments. The charge is that these are not divine communications but retellings of Jewish and Christian lore, acquired through contact with *ahl al-kitāb* (the People of the Book) and then read back to Muhammad ﷺ as though they were new.

The detail "morning and evening" (*bukratan wa aṣīlā*) specifies the method. Someone — the unnamed helpers of 25:4 — is said to write the stories down in advance, then present them to the Prophet at regular intervals so that he can memorize and recite them. The picture is one of a rehearsed performance, not a spontaneous revelation. Al-Ṭabarī connects this with a specific figure from the historical record: al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, a Qurayshī storyteller who would recite tales from Persian history and legend, after which the disbelievers would compare his material with the Quran and declare, in the Prophet's presence, that al-Naḍr's stories were superior. The accusation in 25:5 is, in practice, an extension of this comparison: the Quran's narratives are no different from what any well-read storyteller could produce.

**The Internal Contradiction of the Two Charges**

This pattern — recording the objection and letting its internal weakness show — is a hallmark of the sūrah's method. The disbelievers are not refuted by counterargument alone; they are refuted by the accumulation of their own inconsistencies. The reader is trusted to notice that the same people who say "he invented it" in 25:4 say "he copied it" in 25:5, and to conclude that neither charge can stand on its own, and together they cancel each other out.

**The Surah's Pattern: Objection, Then Answer**

The pairing of 25:4 and 25:5 establishes a pattern the sūrah will follow throughout. Objections are stated fully, often in the disbelievers' own words — *wa qālu*, "and they say" — and then answered. But the answers do not always come immediately. After these two verses of accusation, 25:6 offers a compressed reply: the Quran comes from the Knower of all secrets in the heavens and earth. The full answer unfolds across the next thirty verses: the Prophet's humanity is not a deficiency (25:7-9, 25:20), the promise of the Hereafter is real (25:10-16), the false gods will testify against their worshippers (25:17-19), and the Quran's gradual revelation is deliberate and serves the Prophet's heart (25:32). The disbelievers' objections are given pride of place at the start because the sūrah's purpose is to answer them. A reader who encounters the accusations first understands why the rest of the chapter exists.

The accusation required the audience to believe both that the Prophet was unlettered (which the Qur'an itself affirms in 7:157) and that he was simultaneously conducting an intensive course of study in scriptural literature.
verses.6:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “This ˹Quran˺ has been revealed by the One Who knows the secrets of the heavens and the earth. Surely He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

**Sirr: The Secret That No Helper Could Supply**

The word *sirr* (secret, hidden thing) appears here in the plural — *asrār* — covering everything concealed in the heavens and the earth. The charge in 25:4 was that unnamed helpers provided the Prophet ﷺ with material. The charge in 25:5 was that ancient written sources supplied the content. This verse answers both by pointing to a domain no helper can enter: the unseen. The Quran contains knowledge of events the Prophet ﷺ could not have witnessed — the creation of the heavens, the fate of earlier nations, the interior states of the human soul — and attributes this knowledge to its divine source. If the content exceeds what any human collaborator could know, the collaboration theory collapses.

**Forgiveness After Judgment**

The verse closes with an attribute pair that has puzzled some readers: *innahu kāna ghafūran raḥīmā* — "Surely He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful." After asserting that He knows all secrets — which includes the secrets of the disbelievers' hearts, their plots and their mockery — the verse names forgiveness and mercy. The placement is deliberate. The One who could punish the disbelievers for their accusations against His revelation chooses to announce His willingness to forgive. This is not softness; it is a final offer. The sūrah will describe the punishment in detail (25:11-16), but before the description begins, the door to repentance is left open.

The same pattern appears in 6:54: "Your Lord has prescribed mercy for Himself, so that whoever among you does evil out of ignorance and then repents and does good — He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful." The tension between omniscience and mercy is the Qur'an's persistent theme. God knows what the disbelievers conceal; He does not need their confession to judge them. Yet He offers forgiveness before the judgment arrives. This is the theological structure that makes human responsibility real: the punishment is not inevitable, because the mercy precedes it, but the mercy can be refused, and refusal has consequences.

**The Command to Say: The Prophet as Messenger, Not Author**

The word *qul* — "Say" — appears over three hundred times in the Qur'an, and each appearance performs the same function: it separates the Prophet ﷺ from the message he delivers. He is not the author of the statement; he is the commanded speaker. In 25:6, this matters because the disbelievers' charge was precisely that he was the author. The response — *qul* — denies the premise. If God commands the Prophet to say these words, the Prophet did not compose them. The grammatical form of the command makes the separation visible within the text itself. Every reader encounters *qul* and knows that the sentence that follows belongs to God, not to the man who speaks it aloud. The command to "say" is itself the answer to the charge of fabrication: the speaker and the author are different, and the text makes that difference explicit every time *qul* appears.
verses.7:
> And they say ˹mockingly˺, “What kind of messenger is this who eats food and goes about in market-places ˹for a living˺? If only an angel had been sent down with him to be his co-warner

**The Disbelief That Demands a Different Messenger**

The objection shifts from the message to the messenger. The disbelievers no longer argue about whether the Quran is fabricated or borrowed; they now question whether the person delivering it could possibly be God's chosen envoy. The complaint is double: he eats food, and he walks in the markets. Both are markers of ordinary human life, and both are presented as disqualifications. A real messenger, in their view, should not need sustenance and should not be seen conducting business among common people. The logic is that divine authority and human normalcy are incompatible — a being who needs to eat cannot carry a message from the One who needs nothing.

The people of Noah said, "He is only a human being like you who wants to be superior to you" (23:24). The people of ʿĀd said of their messenger, "You are only a human being like us" (26:154). The Quraysh's version adds a specifically Meccan detail: the market-place. In Makkah, social status was closely tied to wealth and commercial success. The second part of the objection — "If only an angel had been sent down with him" — reveals what the disbelievers actually wanted: visible, physical confirmation of divine authority. An angel co-warner would have served as credentials, a supernatural endorsement that no human messenger could provide alone. This desire recurs in 6:8-9, where the disbelievers say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" and the Qur'an responds, "Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not be reprieved" (6:8). The answer there reveals the hidden consequence of the demand: if an angel appeared, the era of testing would end immediately, because the evidence would be so overwhelming that denial would become impossible. The disbelievers were asking for the very thing that would end their opportunity to choose.

**The Word "Co-Warner" and What It Reveals**

The phrase *nadīran maʿahu* — "a warner with him" or "a co-warner" — deserves separate attention because of what it concedes. The disbelievers do not deny that the Prophet is a warner; they deny that he is enough alone. The word *nadīr* (warner) is the same word used in 25:1 to describe the Prophet's mission — "so that he may be a warner to the whole world." The disbelievers, in the very act of rejecting him, repeat the Qur'an's own description of his function. They accept the category; they reject the person. This is a subtler form of denial than outright rejection: it says, in practice, "we believe in warning. We do not believe you are the one doing it correctly." The demand for an angel co-warner is thus a demand for mediation — for someone else to verify the warning before it is accepted. The Qur'an's response is that the warning stands on its own, delivered by a human being chosen by God, and no co-signer is required. The demand for authentication is itself a form of rejection, because it places a condition on obedience that God has not set.
verses.8:
> or a treasure had been cast down to him, or he had had a garden from which he may eat!” And the wrongdoers say ˹to the believers˺, “You are only following a bewitched man.”

**Wealth and Land as Divine Credentials**

The disbelievers continue their list of what a real messenger should have. Having demanded an angel in 25:7, they now demand material signs: a treasure sent down from heaven and a garden from which the messenger can eat. The pattern of the demand reveals the values at work. In seventh-century Makkah, authority was measured by two visible markers: accumulated wealth and landed property. A man who had neither could not, in the social logic of the Quraysh, claim superiority over those who had both. The request for a treasure (*kanz*) and a garden (*jannah*) is not a request for proof of divine mission; it is a request for the social credentials the audience already respects. The disbelievers are not asking for a sign from God; they are asking for a sign that conforms to their own standards.

The parallel in 43:53 records a similar demand about Moses: "Why were armlets of gold not cast upon him, or angels not accompanying him?" The structure is identical: the messenger lacks what the audience considers necessary for authority, and the lack is treated as disproof of the message. Sūrah 6:111 makes the point explicitly: "Even if We had sent down to them the angels. The dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered all things before them, they still would not have believed — unless Allah had willed." The disbelievers in 25:8 are asking for evidence, but the evidence they want is designed to satisfy a criterion they invented, not one God set.

**The Charge of Bewitchment**

The verse's final clause shifts the accusation to a different register: *mashūr* — bewitched. After calling the Prophet a fabricator (25:4), a borrower of ancient tales (25:5), and an ordinary man unworthy of prophethood (25:7), the disbelievers add one more label: he is under a spell. This is not a casual insult; it is a try to explain the Quran's undeniable effect on its listeners. The Qur'an moved people to tears, to conversion, to a willingness to abandon their families and their tribal allegiances. If it was not divine, and it was not ordinary human speech, some third explanation was needed. Sorcery filled the gap.

The charge appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in the mouths of other communities: the people of Pharaoh accused Moses of sorcery (10:76; 20:63; 26:34), and the people of ʿĀd accused their messenger of bewitchment (7:66). In pre-Islamic Arabia, sorcery was taken seriously as a real phenomenon, not merely as a metaphor for eloquence. To call someone *mashūr* was to place him in a dangerous category — one that could justify violence, since a sorcerer was understood to be a genuine threat to the community. The accusation against the Prophet ﷺ carried social consequences for everyone around him: anyone who followed a bewitched man could be accused of being bewitched themselves, or of complicity in sorcery.

**The Parallel in Saul and the Demand for Signs**

The disbelievers' demand for wealth and material proof before accepting the Prophet echoes a pattern found earlier in the Qur'an's account of the Israelites. In 2:247, when Samuel anointed Saul (Ṭālūt) as king, the Israelites objected: "How can he have authority over us when we are more worthy of authority than him. He has not been given abundant wealth?" The objection is structurally identical to the one in 25:8: a man is chosen by God for leadership, and the people reject him because he lacks the material markers they associate with authority. The Qur'an's response to the Israelites was that God had chosen Saul and given him knowledge and stature; the response to the Quraysh, stated in 25:10, is that God can give far better than what they demand. The pattern repeats across prophetic history because the error is the same: measuring spiritual authority by material wealth, and rejecting what God chooses because it does not match what humans prefer.
verses.9:
> See ˹O Prophet˺ how they call you names! So they have gone so ˹far˺ astray that they cannot find the ˹Right˺ Way

**A Verse of Divine Observation**

The verse turns away from the disbelievers and speaks directly to the Prophet ﷺ: *unẓur kayfaḍarabū laka'l-amthāl* — "Look how they set forth their parables about you." The command to "see" is not an invitation to gather evidence or construct a response. It is a divine observation offered to the Prophet as consolation. God is showing him the absurdity of his opponents' position. They have called him a fabricator, a borrower of tales, an ordinary man unworthy of prophethood, and a sorcerer — all in the space of five verses — and each label contradicts the others. The purpose of *unẓur* is not to instruct the Prophet but to reassure him: the disbelievers' confusion is visible, and it is self-inflicted.

The word *amthāl* (parables, comparisons, descriptions) is significant. The Qur'an calls these *amthāl* — a word it reserves elsewhere for the illustrative parables God Himself sets forth (e.g., 2:26; 13:17; 24:35).

**The Prophetic Response to Mockery**

The tone of this verse is instructive for understanding the Qur'an's guidance to the Prophet ﷺ in the face of sustained ridicule. The divine instruction is not "argue back" or "defend yourself" or "produce a sign." It is "look." The Prophet is invited to observe his opponents' confusion from the perspective of one who already knows the truth. This posture — observation rather than reaction — appears elsewhere in the Qur'an's address to the Prophet. In 6:176: "Do not grieve over those who rush into disbelief." In 15:97: "We certainly know that your heart is distressed by what they say." The emotional reality is acknowledged, but the strategic instruction is the same: observe, do not be consumed.

**The Sūrah's Structural Placement of the Verse**

Verse 25:9 occupies a specific structural position: it is the last verse before the sūrah shifts from describing the disbelievers' objections to describing their consequences. The next verse (25:10) turns from the disbelievers' accusations to God's promise of gardens and palaces, and from there the sūrah moves into its extended Last-Day passage (25:11-19). The placement of 25:9 at this hinge point is deliberate. The sūrah has given the disbelievers five verses to make their case — fabrication, copying, bewitchment, demands for signs — and now it pauses to pronounce judgment on their method before moving to the consequences. The pause is brief: one verse, one observation, one diagnosis. But it serves as the closing argument of the prosecution before the sentencing begins. The disbelievers have spoken; the sūrah has recorded their words faithfully; and now it pronounces, in God's voice, that those words have led the speakers nowhere. What follows — the fire, the garden, the courtroom — is the result of the path the disbelievers chose when they lost the ability to find any other way. The verse's placement is the sūrah's way of saying: the case is closed, and the verdict is in.
verses.10:
> Blessed is the One Who—if He wills—can give you far better than ˹all˺ that: gardens under which rivers flow, and palaces as well

**The Response to Material Demands**

The disbelievers had demanded a treasure and a garden for the Prophet ﷺ in 25:8 — material signs that would confirm his prophethood in terms the Quraysh understood. God's answer does not provide those signs. Instead, it promises something better: gardens with rivers beneath them and palaces (*quṣūr*). The promise is not directed at the disbelievers who demanded the signs but at the Prophet who endured the demand. The shift from the audience's terms to God's terms is the verse's central move.

The word *tabāraka* ("Blessed") opens the verse as it opened the sūrah in 25:1, creating a structural echo. The "if He wills" (*in shā'a*) introduces divine discretion — the promise is not automatic but contingent on God's will, a theological point that keeps the relationship between human effort and divine gift in tension. The phrase *in shā'a* does not introduce doubt; it affirms freedom — God promises from freedom, not from obligation, and a promise made freely is more reliable than one made under compulsion.

**Quṣūr: Palaces as a Marker of Restoration**

The word *quṣūr* (palaces, mansions) appears in several Qur'anic passages describing Paradise. In 7:74, it refers to the stone dwellings built by the Thamūd, the people of Ṣāliḥ — a historical usage that grounds the word in material reality before applying it to the Last-Day context. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr note that for the Quraysh, *quṣūr* meant any dwelling made of stone, which was a mark of permanence and status in a society where most structures were made of mud and palm fronds. The promise of palaces in Paradise thus uses the audience's own standard of luxury and exceeds it.

In 22:45 — "How many a city We have destroyed while it was doing wrong, lying in ruins, with abandoned wells and lofty palaces" — the *quṣūr* are ruins, testimony to the impermanence of worldly power. The word in 25:10 reverses that image: the palaces God promises are permanent, not because stone endures but because the One who builds them does not allow decay. The contrast between the ruined palaces of destroyed cities and the eternal palaces of Paradise is implicit in the Qur'an's use of the same word across different contexts. The disbelievers who demanded a garden and a treasure in 25:8 are offered something their language already contains but their imagination could not reach.

**Why the Promise Comes Before the Warning**

The sequence of the sūrah is instructive. After five verses of accusation (25:4-8) and one verse of observation (25:9), the next response is not a warning but a promise. The garden and the palace come before the fire and the chains. This ordering is not accidental; it reflects the Qur'an's consistent preference for attraction over fear as the primary mode of persuasion. The warning will follow — 25:11 introduces the denial of the Hour and the preparation of the Blaze — but the promise comes first. The reader encounters the possibility of reward before the reality of punishment, and the reward is framed in terms the audience already desires: flowing water, permanent homes, a life without want.

> In fact, they deny the Hour. And for the deniers of the Hour, We have prepared a blazing Fire

**The Root Diagnosis**

The sūrah identifies what is really wrong with the disbelievers. After cataloguing their objections — fabrication, borrowed tales, bewitchment, demands for material signs — the text names the underlying condition: *bal kadhdhabū bi's-sā'ah* — "In fact, they deny the Hour." The word *bal* ("in fact," "rather") functions as a correction. Everything the disbelievers have said — the accusations, the mockery, the demands — is surface. The real problem is not that they find the Prophet inadequate or the Quran unconvincing; it is that they reject the reality of accountability after death. Every objection is an expression of that rejection dressed in different clothes. If there is no Hour, there is no consequence; if there is no consequence, the messenger is unnecessary; if the messenger is unnecessary, the message can be dismissed. The verse strips away the arguments and exposes the foundation.

The Hour (*al-sā'ah*) is the Qur'an's term for the moment the created order ends and the Day of Judgment begins. It appears throughout the Qur'an as the single event the disbelievers most consistently deny: "They seek to hasten the Hour" (42:18); "The disbelievers are in doubt about the Hour" (41:54); "Woe on that Day to those who deny" (77:15). The denial is not incidental but structural to their worldview. If the Hour is real, everything changes: wealth is temporary, status is meaningless, and the man who walks in the markets carrying a message from God is more important than the kings who mock him. The denial of the Hour is the denial of the entire moral architecture the Quran is building, and the sūrah names it here as the root from which all other objections grow.

**Saʿīr: The Blaze Prepared in Advance**

The verse describes the punishment for denial as *saʿīr* — a blazing fire, a kindled flame. The word is used across the Qur'an as a near-synonym for *nār* (fire) but carries an additional intensity: *saʿīr* is fire that has been set alight deliberately, fire with agency. The term appears in 4:10, 4:55, 17:97, 22:4, 31:21, 33:64, 35:6, 42:7, 48:13, 67:5, 67:10, 67:11, 76:4, and 84:12. Its recurrence across diverse contexts — warnings to the disbelievers, descriptions of the Day, assurances to the Prophet — makes it one of the Qur'an's primary vocabulary items for the punishment of the Hereafter.

**Denial as the Engine of Every Other Error**

The verse's placement after the catalogue of objections is deliberate. By naming the denial of the Hour as the root, the sūrah reorders the disbelievers' arguments. The charge of fabrication (25:4) is not about evidence; it is about the refusal to accept that accountability exists. The demand for a treasure (25:8) is not about proof; it is about the assumption that material success is the only measure of worth, an assumption that collapses if the Hereafter is real. The accusation of bewitchment (25:8) is not about the Prophet's character; it is about the need to explain away an effect they cannot accept, because accepting it would mean accepting the source.

This diagnosis — that all objections reduce to one denial — is the sūrah's interpretive key. The rest of the chapter will describe the consequences of that denial in escalating detail: the fire will see them from afar (25:12), they will be compressed in a narrow space (25:13), they will call for destruction upon destruction (25:14).
verses.12:
> Once it sees them from a distance, they will hear it fuming and growling

**Hell as a Living Presence**

The verse uses a striking grammatical construction: the fire sees. *Idhā ra'athum min makānin baʿīd* — "When it sees them from a place far off." Hell is not described as a passive location; it is given the faculty of sight. This animation of the fire is one of the most vivid features of the Qur'anic the doctrine of the Last Day. The fire has perception, and it perceives its victims before they arrive. The grammar places Hell as the subject of the verb "to see," making it an agent rather than a destination. The disbelievers do not enter Hell; Hell perceives them. The difference is enormous: a place can be escaped from; a perceiving entity has already made contact.

Al-Qurṭubī records a ḥadīth portraying the Fire as a sentient being on the Day of Resurrection — endowed with vision, hearing, and speech — that will seize the polytheists as swiftly as a bird swallows a seed. The theological debate over whether these attributes should be understood literally or metaphorically divides the Muʿtazilites, who reject such corporeal descriptions, from those who accept that God can endue the fire with whatever faculties He wills. The ḥadīth, reported by al-Qurṭubī through multiple chains, gives the fire agency that goes beyond what the verse requires but does not contradict it.

**The Sounds of the Fire**

The Qur'an's use of sound to convey the horror of Hell appears in other passages as well. In 67:7 — "When they are thrown into it, they hear its roaring as it boils" — the sound is produced by the fire at the moment of contact. In 25:12, the sound precedes contact, creating a different psychological effect: dread before the experience, fear of something that has not yet arrived but is clearly coming. The extended approach multiplies the torment: the disbelievers spend the approach listening to what awaits them, and every step closer brings a louder growl.

**The Graduated Architecture of Dread**

The verse's contribution to the sūrah's Last-Day sequence is the concept of graduated approach. The punishment of Hell as the Qur'an describes it is not a single event but a process, and 25:12 captures the first stage: perception at a distance. The disbelievers are still far from the fire, but they can hear it — its rage, its growling — and the hearing begins the punishment before the heat does. This graduated approach appears in other Qur'anic passages as well. In 32:12 — "If only you could see when the criminals will hang their heads before their Lord" — the humiliation precedes the sentencing. In 77:25-30 — "Woe on that Day to the deniers! Did We not make the earth a resting place, and the mountains as stakes?" — the questioning precedes the punishment. The Qur'an's the doctrine of the Last Day is never instantaneous; it is always staged, because staging extends the experience of consequence across time, and time in Hell is itself part of the punishment.

In 14:50 — "Their garment will be of boiling fluid, and the Fire will cover their faces" — the punishment is physical and immediate.

> And when they are tossed into a narrow place inside ˹Hell˺, chained together, then and there they will cry out for ˹instant˺ destruction

**Compression After the Roar**

The description of Hell escalates from sound to confinement. Verse 25:12 gave the fire a voice; verse 25:13 places the disbelievers inside it — not in an open expanse but in a *makān ḍayyiq*, a narrow, cramped space. The Arabic root *ḍ-y-q* conveys constriction, suffocation, the inability to move freely. The fire does not merely surround them; it presses against them from every side. The effect is the opposite of what the disbelievers valued in life: they were people who measured authority by spaciousness — gardens, palaces, open markets — and the punishment strips that away completely. What remains is closeness without comfort, proximity without intimacy, and pressure without relief.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have described the constriction using the image of a spearhead forced into the shaft of a spear — a thing compressed so tightly that no gap remains. The metaphor conveys both the tightness and the force: the bodies inside the narrow place are not settling naturally; they are packed in, pushed together by an external power. The passive verb *ulqū* ("they are tossed") removes the last trace of agency. They do not walk into the narrow place; they are thrown. The throwing is itself a humiliation — the disbelievers who walked proudly in the markets of Makkah, who expected their Prophet to meet their standards of dignity, are now handled without regard for their preference or their pride.

**Muqarranīn: Chained Together**

The word *qarana* (to bind, to join, to chain) appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in a different register. In 4:36 — "Do not join one sin with another" — the word describes a moral binding: the accumulation of wrongs. In 25:13, the binding is physical, but the echo of the moral usage is not accidental.

**The Active Fire and the Passive Human**

The grammar of 25:13 reinforces the reversal of power described in 25:12. In life, the disbelievers were agents: they chose their gods, they demanded their signs, they mocked the Prophet, they shaped the social world of Makkah according to their preferences. In the narrow place, they are objects. The verb *ulqū* ("they are tossed") is passive; the subject who tosses is unnamed, presumably God or His angels. The disbelievers do not walk, do not choose, do not act. They are acted upon. The word *muqarranīn* ("chained together") reinforces the passivity: they cannot separate, cannot move, cannot even choose their companions in punishment. The contrast with their former agency is total. In Makkah, they moved freely through markets and gathering places, controlled their social environment, and shaped their identities through their choices. In the narrow place, every freedom has been removed, and what remains is the bare human being, stripped of status, stripped of movement, stripped of the ability to act. The punishment is not only pain; it is the removal of everything the disbelievers used to define themselves.

> ˹They will be told,˺ “Do not cry only once for destruction, but cry many times over!”

**Why the Verse Matters Theologically**

The denial of the cry for destruction establishes a theological principle: the punishment of the Hereafter is not corrective. It does not reform the punished; it does not lead to a better state. In this world, suffering can produce growth, repentance, or at least endurance. In the Hereafter as the Qur'an describes it, suffering produces only the desire for more suffering to end — a desire that is itself denied. The distinction between worldly and otherworldly punishment is one the Qur'an makes explicit elsewhere: "The punishment of the Hereafter is more terrible and more lasting" (20:127). The word "more lasting" (*aqām*) establishes that the punishment endures, and 25:14 confirms that it endures without interruption.

**The Qur'an's Recurring Theme of Unending Punishment**

The concept of punishment without relief appears throughout the Qur'an in various formulations. In 4:56 — "Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment" — the renewal is physical: the body is destroyed and reconstituted so that it can suffer again. In 20:74 — "Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell, where he neither dies nor lives" — the punishment occupies a space between death and life, denying both. In 78:23-25 — "They will remain in it for ages; they will not taste any coolness or any drink, except boiling fluid and dark, murky filth" — the duration is specified as ages (*ḥuqub*, periods of time so long they become indistinguishable from eternity).

The statement in 25:14 adds a distinct tone: it is spoken directly to the victims, in their own words, turned against them. They asked for destruction; the answer uses their word — *thubūr* — and multiplies it. The rhetorical technique is one the Qur'an employs in several Last-Day passages: the disbelievers' own speech is quoted back to them, reframed. In 23:107-108, the people of Hell say, "Our Lord, remove us from it. If we return to evil, then we will be wrongdoers," and the response is, "Remain despised in it, and do not speak to Me." In 25:14, the response is not silence but amplification: you asked for destruction once; here is destruction upon destruction.

**The Sūrah's Place in the Qur'an's Last-Day Tradition**

Verse 25:14 belongs to a family of Qur'anic passages that describe the disbelievers' response to Hell with the same mixture of despair and denial. In 35:36-37, the people of Hell say, "Our Lord, remove us and we will do righteous deeds, not what we used to do," and the response is, "Did We not give you a lifespan in which anyone who would take heed could have done so? And the warner came to you, so taste it." In 43:77, they cry out, "O Mālik, let your Lord finish us off," and Mālik replies, "You will remain." The pattern is consistent: the people in Hell ask for an end, and the answer is that there is no end. The verse in 25:14 fits this pattern exactly. The disbelievers' request for destruction is turned into a command to request more destruction, and the command is itself the punishment. The multiplication of the request is the multiplication of the suffering, and the suffering does not resolve.

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Is this better or the Garden of Eternity which the righteous have been promised, as a reward and ˹an ultimate˺ destination

**The Rhetorical Turn**

After four verses of unbroken description of Hell — the fire that sees (25:12), the narrow confinement (25:13), the denial of annihilation (25:14) — the sūrah pivots with a question addressed to the Prophet: *qul*, "Say." The question is one the audience is meant to answer for themselves: "Is this better, or the Garden of Eternity which the righteous have been promised?" The word *this* (*dhālik*) refers to everything described in 25:11-14: the fire, the compression, the chains, the multiplied destruction. The Garden of Eternity is presented as its opposite: not confinement but spaciousness, not destruction but permanence, not chains but rest. The question does not need an answer in the text; the answer is self-evident, and the verse's power lies in the audience's forced recognition that the self-evident answer is available only through the path the disbelievers have rejected.

The technique — a question whose answer condemns the questioner — is one the Qur'an uses in several passages. In 87:16-17: "But you prefer the life of this world. The Hereafter is better and more lasting." In 9:38: "What is the matter with you that when you are told, 'Go forth in the cause of Allah,' you cling heavily to the earth?" The question in 25:15 does not argue; it places side by side. The reader sees both outcomes side by side and must choose. The contrast is the argument, and the argument requires nothing beyond the two options laid out in the same sentence.

**Khuld: The Eternity That Gives the Garden Its Name**

The word *khuld* (eternity, everlastingness) is the same root from which the verb *khālidīn* ("abiding") comes in 25:16. It means "to remain," "to stay," and when applied to the Hereafter it carries the force of permanence without end. The Garden is not a temporary reward that expires; it is a state that continues. This is the feature that distinguishes it from every earthly garden, every human pleasure, every material satisfaction — all of which are subject to time. The disbelievers asked for a garden in 25:8; the Garden promised here exceeds their request in kind, not merely in degree.

Al-Rāzī observes that the word *khuld* applies to both Paradise and Hell. The theological debate about whether the punishment is truly eternal or whether it might eventually end is addressed by the use of *khuld* in passages like 4:93: "Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his reward is Hell, in which he will abide forever (*khālidan fīhā*)." The permanence is stated as a fact, not a possibility.

**The Bridge to 25:16**

The verse ends with a question mark, and the answer comes in 25:16, which describes the contents of the Garden: "There they will have whatever they wish for, forever." The bridge between the two verses is the word *mawʿūd* ("promised"), which appears in 25:15. The promise itself is part of the argument: the righteous have been told what awaits them, and the telling is a moral act — it makes the choice between the fire and the garden a conscious one. The disbelievers were offered the same choice and chose differently. The sūrah's structure places the two options — fire (25:11-14) and garden (25:15-16) — in the same breath, and the reader must decide which word resonates louder: *thubūr* (destruction) or *khuld* (eternity).

The word *muttaqīn* appears throughout the Qur'an as the defining quality of those who receive God's favor: "The Book, in which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-conscious" (2:2); "Be conscious of Allah, and know that you will meet Him" (2:233).

> There they will have whatever they wish for, forever. That is a promise ˹to be sought after˺, binding on your Lord.”

**The Content of the Garden: Unlimited and Permanent**

The verse describes what awaits the righteous inside the Garden of Eternity named in 25:15: *lahum fīhā mā yashā'ūna khālidīn* — "There they will have whatever they wish for, forever." The phrasing is comprehensive. It does not list specific blessings — rivers of milk, fruits of every kind, silk garments — though these appear elsewhere in the Qur'an (47:15; 56:20-23; 76:21). Instead, it grants the wish itself: whatever the inhabitant desires, that is what exists. This is a promise without specification, which means it is also without limit. The Qur'an makes this point explicit in 39:34: "They will have whatever they desire with their Lord. That is the reward of the doers of good." The same wording appears in 16:31; 42:22; and 50:35, each time reinforcing the principle: Paradise is not a place with a fixed menu but a place where the desire and the fulfillment are identical.

The word *khālidīn* ("forever," literally "abiding") ties this verse to the *khuld* of 25:15. The Garden is eternal not only in its existence but in its provision: the wish does not diminish, the fulfillment does not tire, and the eternity does not become monotonous. This last point matters because the human experience of satisfaction is always temporary — what delights at first ceases to delight with repetition. The Qur'an's promise of eternal fulfillment implies a change in the nature of the one who wishes, not merely an abundance of the things wished for. The inhabitants of the Garden are not the same as they were in the world; they have been purified, and their desires have been purified with them. The wish and the wished-for are both transformed.

**The Simplicity of the Promise**

What the Garden contains, according to 25:16, is not a list but a principle: *mā yashā'ūna* — "whatever they wish for." The simplicity is deliberate. The Qur'an elsewhere describes Paradise in elaborate detail — rivers of water, milk, wine, and honey (47:15); fruits of every kind (56:20-23); silk garments and bracelets of gold (76:21); couches arranged in rows (56:15-16). In 25:16, none of these are mentioned. The verse reduces the entire content of Paradise to a single phrase: whatever the inhabitant desires. This reduction is not vagueness; it is the ultimate specification. A list of blessings can be exhausted; a wish cannot. The promise is not that Paradise contains a set number of pleasures but that every desire, including desires that have not yet been imagined, will be fulfilled. The *forever* that follows (*khālidīn*) ensures that the fulfillment does not diminish: what is wished for at the first moment is available at the last, and there is no last moment. The simplicity of the verse is its strength: it promises everything by naming the principle rather than the particulars.
verses.17:
> ˹Watch for˺ the Day He will gather them along with what they used to worship besides Allah, and ask ˹the objects of worship˺, “Was it you who misled these servants of Mine, or did they stray from the Way ˹on their own˺?”

**The Word ʿIbād: God Names Them His Servants**

A subtle but devastating detail in the verse is God's use of the word *'ibād* — "servants" — to describe the disbelievers. The same people who served other gods are here called God's servants, because in the Qur'anic framework, all created beings are God's servants regardless of what they worship. The disbelievers served idols, but they remained God's servants; their worship of others did not transfer them to another owner. The word *'ibādī* ("My servants") establishes God's claim over them and makes the question more pointed: "Was it you who misled *My* servants?" The false gods are being asked about their actions toward beings who belonged to God, not to them.

In 15:49 — "Inform My servants that I am the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful" — the same word *'ibādī* appears in a context of mercy. In 25:17, it appears in a context of judgment.

**The Parallel in 5:116**

The scene in 25:17 closely parallels the interrogation of Jesus in 5:116: "And when Allah said, 'O Jesus, son of Mary! Did you say to people, "Take me and my mother as gods besides Allah?"' he said, 'Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say.'" The structure is identical: God asks the object of worship whether it encouraged the worship; the object denies it. The two passages together establish an universal principle: no being that was worshipped besides God will stand on the Day of Judgment as a co-defendant with its worshippers. Every false god will testify against those who worshipped it.

The identity of the objects of worship in 25:17 is specified by the commentators. Al-Qurṭubī includes angels, jinn, idols, and Jesus among the possibilities, noting that the verse is general enough to encompass every form of *shirk* (associating others with God) that has occurred in human history. The verse does not name the false gods because it does not need to; the question applies to all of them without exception. The generality is the point: the question covers every object of false worship that has ever existed, and the answer will be the same for each one. The scene in 25:17-18 will record those answers, and they will be unanimous: "Glory be to You! It was not right for us to take any lords besides You.".

**The Excluded Defense**

The structure of God's question in 25:17 leaves no room for a third option. The question offers two possibilities: either the objects of worship misled the disbelievers, or the disbelievers strayed on their own. There is no third answer — no "we were confused," no "the evidence was unclear," no "we did our best with what we had." The binary framing eliminates every form of excuse that falls between deception and willful error. The disbelievers cannot claim that the objects of worship were partly responsible and they were partly responsible, because the question does not allow shared blame. Each party is held to account for its own role: the objects of worship for what they did or did not do, and the disbelievers for what they chose. The courtroom of the Day of Judgment, as 25:17 presents it, does not accept ambiguous verdicts. The question forces a clear answer, and the clear answer forces a clear consequence.
verses.18:
> They will say, “Glory be to You! It was not right for ˹others like˺ us to take any lords besides You, but You allowed enjoyment for them and their forefathers ˹for so long˺ that they forgot ˹Your˺ remembrance and became a doomed people.”

**The Forefathers and the Mechanism of Forgetfulness**

The false gods continue their testimony with a diagnosis of how the misguidance occurred. It was not their doing; it was a process set in motion by *tamattuʿ* — "enjoyment" or "provision" — that God granted to the disbelievers and their forefathers over a long period. The word *mattaʿnā* ("We granted enjoyment") is significant because it places the provision of worldly goods within God's own action, not the false gods'. God gave them life, sustenance, time, and comfort. The result was not gratitude but amnesia: *fa-nsū'dh-dhikr* — "they forgot the remembrance." The remembrance (*dhikr*) they forgot is God Himself — His rights, His commands, His presence.

This mechanism — that prolonged comfort produces spiritual amnesia — appears throughout the Qur'an. In 20:124-126, God says of the one who turns away from His remembrance: "We will give him a life of hardship." In 17:67: "When adversity touches you at sea, lost are those you invoke except Him. But when He delivers you to land, you turn away." The false gods in 25:18 are citing the same pattern: God provided, humans forgot, and the forgetting became the basis for the misguidance they are now being asked about. The *forefathers* are mentioned because the pattern was inherited: the first generation forgot, and the second generation inherited the forgetting as custom. What began as spiritual negligence became cultural practice, and cultural practice became identity. By the time the disbelievers worshipped idols in Makkah, they were not making a theological choice; they were continuing what their fathers had done, and their fathers had forgotten why.

**"A Doomed People" and the Problem of Overextension**

The final phrase — *wa kānū qawman buwrā* — translates as "and they became a doomed people." The word *buwrā* means ruined, lost, beyond recovery. It describes not a single act of sin but a condition — a people who have gone so far into misguidance that correction from within is no longer possible. The false gods' testimony is that this condition was self-inflicted. They did not cause it; they did not encourage it; they stood by while the disbelievers brought it upon themselves through the slow process of forgetting God in the midst of His blessings.

The disbelievers accused the Prophet ﷺ of fabrication (25:4), bewitchment (25:8), and ordinary humanity (25:7). The false gods' confession is the mirror image of the disbelievers' denial: the objects of worship say *subḥānaka* (Glory be to You), and in doing so they model the response the disbelievers should have given but refused.

**The Inheritance of Error and the Break in the Chain**

The Qur'an breaks this chain by insisting that each individual is responsible for their own belief. "No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38). The forefathers' error is the context, not the excuse. The false gods' testimony in 25:18 names the forefathers not to transfer blame but to explain the origin: the error began with a generation that forgot, and it continued because the next generation did not ask why. The Day of Judgment separates the inheritors from their inheritance and holds each person accountable for what they did with the life they were given — not what their fathers did with theirs.
verses.19:
> ˹The doomed will be told˺, “Your gods have clearly denied your claims. So now you can neither ward off ˹the punishment˺ nor get any help.” And whoever of you does wrong, We will make them taste a horrible punishment

**The Verdict After the Testimony**

The verse delivers God's ruling after the false gods have testified in 25:18. The disbelievers are addressed directly: *faqad kadhdhabūkum* — "Your gods have clearly denied your claims." The word *kadhdhabūkum* is the same root used throughout the sūrah for the disbelievers' rejection of the Prophet: they called him a liar (*kadhdhabū*) in 25:4, 25:5, and 25:11. Now the same charge is turned against them — not by a human messenger but by the very beings they worshipped. The false gods have called the disbelievers liars, and the disbelievers have no rebuttal. The symmetry is devastating: the people who denied the truth are now themselves denied by the objects of their misplaced devotion. The word *kadhdhabū* does not change; only the direction changes.

The statement that follows — *fa-mā taṣṭī'ūna ḍarran wa-lā naṣrā* — "So now you can neither ward off the punishment nor get any help" — removes both strategies simultaneously. *Ḍarr* means to avert, to push away; *naṣr* means assistance, help from an ally. The tribal networks that pressured the believers in Makkah are dissolved. Every social, political, and spiritual resource the disbelievers relied on has evaporated, and what remains is the individual standing alone before the One whose sovereignty was declared in 25:2.

**The Individual Within the Collective**

The final clause — *wa-man yaẓlim minkum nūdhiquhu ʿadhāban kabīrān* — introduces an individual register into a passage that has been addressing the disbelievers as a group. "Whoever among you does wrong" (*man yaẓlim minkum*) singles out each person. The punishment is not collective by default; it is assigned to individuals who chose wrong. This is the Qur'an's consistent position: the Day of Judgment separates people from their groups, their families, their tribes, and their communities. In 6:94 — "You have come to Us alone, as We first created you, leaving behind everything We gave you" — the individuality of the encounter is stated as a fact. In 19:95 — "Every one of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection" — the same principle appears.

**The Penalty for Wrongdoing: Individual and Certain**

The verse ends with an individualized warning: "Whoever among you does wrong, We will make them taste a horrible punishment." The shift from the collective "you" to the individual "whoever" is a standard Qur'anic move at the conclusion of a judgment passage. It ensures that no one in the audience can hide behind the group. The disbelievers addressed in 25:19 are not a mass; they are persons, each of whom made a choice, and each of whom will face the consequence of that choice alone. The word *nūdhiquhu* ("We will make him taste") is visceral: the punishment is not only witnessed or announced but experienced, tasted on the tongue, felt in the body. The Qur'an uses the verb "to taste" for punishment in many passages (3:106; 10:70; 32:21; 78:24), and in each case it insists that the consequence is not abstract but physical, not future but present, not theoretical but certain.
verses.20:
> We never sent any messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺, who did not eat food and go about in market-places. We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you ˹not then˺ be patient? And your Lord is All-Seeing

**The Universal Answer to the Specific Objection**

The verse returns to the objection raised in 25:7 — "What kind of messenger is this who eats food and walks in the markets?" — and answers it by universalizing the charge. Every messenger God sent before Muhammad ﷺ ate food and walked among their people. The phrasing is categorical: *mā arsalnā min qablika min rasūlin illā innahum la-ya'kulūna't-ṭa'ama wa yamtashūna fi'l-aswāq* — "We never sent any messenger before you who did not eat food and go about in market-places." The construction *mā...illā* (none...except) is an universal negative: no exception existed. The disbelievers' demand for a non-human messenger would disqualify every prophet in the chain of revelation, including those the Quraysh acknowledged as genuine — Abraham, Ishmael, Moses, Jesus.

The mention of market-places (*aswāq*) is not incidental. The objection in 25:7 was that the Prophet's humanity disqualified him; the answer in 25:20 is that his humanity qualified every prophet before him.

**Patience as the Appropriate Response**

*Hal anta ṣābirūn* — "Will you be patient?" — is both a question and an implicit command. The Arabic allows both readings: it asks whether the Prophet and the believers are capable of patience, and it instructs them to be patient. The word *ṣabr* in the Qur'an is not passive endurance but active steadfastness — holding one's position against pressure without moving, without compromising, without retaliating in kind. It is the quality the Qur'an most consistently demands of the Prophet ﷺ in the face of opposition: "So be patient, as the messengers of strong resolve were patient" (46:35); "Be patient, for the promise of Allah is true" (40:55).

**Wa Rabbuka Baṣīr: Your Lord Is All-Seeing**

The verse closes with *wa Rabbuka Baṣīr* — "And your Lord is All-Seeing." The word *Baṣīr* names one of God's attributes: the One who sees everything, including the suffering of His prophets and the actions of their oppressors. The statement is a consolation and a warning simultaneously. For the Prophet, it means: God sees what you endure, and your patience is not unnoticed. For the disbelievers, it means: God sees what you do, and your mockery will not be forgotten. The single word *Baṣīr* holds both meanings at once, and the verse allows the reader to feel whichever applies. The attribute appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in similar dual contexts: in 4:58 — "Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners. When you judge between people, to judge with justice" — the instruction to judge justly is followed by "Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing," reminding the judge that his judgment is observed. In 25:20, the observation is aimed at both sides: the patient and the persecutor, the mocked and the mocker. Neither is unseen, and neither is unrecorded.
verses.21:
> Those who do not expect to meet Us say, “If only the angels were sent down to us, or we could see our Lord!” They have certainly been carried away by their arrogance and have entirely exceeded all limits

**The Demand Repeated and the Diagnosis Applied**

The verse returns to the same demand voiced in 25:7 — "If only an angel had been sent down with him" — and restates it with a broader scope: the disbelievers now want angels sent down to them directly, or a visible manifestation of God Himself. The demand has escalated. In 25:7, they asked for an angel to accompany the Prophet as a co-warner; in 25:21, they ask for angels to appear to them personally, or for God to show Himself. The escalation reveals that no amount of evidence would satisfy them, because the demand is not genuine. It is a rhetorical move designed to make faith appear impossible: set the evidentiary bar so high that nothing can clear it, then blame God for not clearing it.

The phrase *alladhīna lā yarjūna liqā'anā* — "those who do not expect to meet Us" — names the root problem, the same diagnosis offered in 25:11: the denial of the Hour. The word *yarjūna* (expect, hope, anticipate) carries a double edge. In its positive sense, it means to hope for something good; in its negative sense, it means to anticipate something feared. The disbelievers do not hope to meet God because they do not believe the meeting will occur. Their demand for angels and a visible Lord is made from within a worldview that assumes there is no reckoning, and therefore the demand can be as extravagant as they wish. If there is no meeting, demanding proof of the meeting costs nothing. The demand to see God directly echoes the most dramatic theophany in the Qur'anic narrative: the request of the Israelites to Moses. In 2:55, they said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until we see God outright." The result was the thunder and lightning that struck them dead, followed by their resurrection. The parallel with 25:21 is structural: in both cases, the demand for visible proof comes from people who have already received enough guidance and are using the demand as a refusal dressed as inquiry.

The disbelievers of Makkah ask for something that is possible in principle — angels can be sent down — but that God has chosen not to do, for reasons the Qur'an has already explained (6:8: if an angel appeared, the matter would be decided, and testing would end).

**The Sūrah's Structural Placement of the Verse**

Verse 25:21 closes the second cycle of disbelievers' objections in the sūrah. The first cycle ran from 25:4 to 25:8 (charges of fabrication, borrowing, bewitchment, demands for material signs); the second cycle opens in 25:21 with a demand for angels or a visible God. The sūrah presents the same pattern twice because the disbelievers' method is repetitive: when one objection is answered, they produce another, using the same underlying logic — the refusal to accept the human messenger and the message he carries. The structural repetition is itself an argument: the disbelievers are not engaging with the evidence; they are cycling through different versions of the same refusal. The sūrah records each version and answers it, but the answers do not produce belief because the problem was never the quality of the answers. The problem, as 25:21 names it, is *istikbār* — arrogance — and arrogance is not defeated by evidence. It is defeated only by the willingness to submit, which is precisely what the disbelievers refuse to do. The verse's placement at the head of the second cycle marks the return of the same disease in a new form, and the sūrah's response — the descriptions of the Day, the angels, the gardens, and the fire — is the same medicine prescribed again.
verses.22:
> ˹But˺ on the Day they will see the angels, there will be no good news for the wicked, who will cry, “Keep away! Away ˹from us˺!”

**The Irony of Fulfilled Demand**

The disbelievers demanded to see the angels in 25:21, and 25:22 delivers the demand — on the Day they will see the angels. The verse opens with *yawma yarawna'l-malā'ikah* — "the Day they will see the angels" — using the same verb (*ra'a*, to see) that the disbelievers used in their demand. The seeing happens. But the context has changed completely. In life, seeing the angels would have been proof that might have led to belief; on the Day of Judgment, seeing the angels is a confirmation of punishment. The demand is fulfilled after the window for belief has closed. This is the Qur'an's consistent treatment of demands for delayed evidence: the evidence arrives when it is too late to act on it.

The phrase *lā bushrā yawma'idhin lil-mujrimīn* — "there will be no good news for the wicked on that Day" — negates the possibility of comfort. The word *bushrā* (good news, glad tidings) appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in contexts of reward: the angels give good news to the righteous at death (16:32; 41:30). For the wicked, the same angels that deliver good news to others deliver dread. The disbelievers' demand in 25:21 was for the angels' appearance as a sign; what they receive is the angels' appearance as a verdict.

**The Day as the Fulfillment of the Unwanted**

The verse contributes to the sūrah's broader pattern of fulfilled demands that produce the opposite of what was intended. The disbelievers demanded gardens and treasure in 25:8; the gardens are promised to the righteous, not to them. They demanded an angel co-warner in 25:7; the angels appear as a threat. They demanded to see God in 25:21; the meeting they avoided will occur on terms they did not choose. The sūrah's architecture turns every demand inside out: what was asked for is given, but in a form that proves the asker wrong. The demand for angels was supposed to produce belief; the appearance of angels produces terror. The demand for material proof was supposed to establish the Prophet's inadequacy; the Hereafter reveals that the Prophet was the adequate one all along.

**The Sūrah’s Pattern of Fulfilled Demands**

Verse 25:22 closes the second cycle of objections in the sūrah. The first cycle ran from 25:4 to 25:8; the second opens in 25:21 with a demand for angels or a visible Lord. The same pattern repeats because the disbelievers’ method is circular: when one objection is answered, another appears, built on the same underlying logic of refusal. The structural repetition is itself an argument: the disbelievers are not engaging with the evidence; they are cycling through variations of the same denial. Each variation is recorded and answered, but the answers do not produce belief because the problem was never the quality of the answers. The problem, as 25:21 names it, is istikbār — arrogance — and arrogance is not defeated by evidence. It is defeated only by the willingness to submit, which is precisely what the disbelievers refuse. The sūrah records the cycle and names the disease, trusting the reader to see that the repetition of objections is itself the proof of bad faith.
verses.23:
> Then We will turn to whatever ˹good˺ deeds they did, reducing them to scattered dust

**The Nullification of Every Work**

The verse describes God's response to the deeds of the disbelievers: *wa qallibnā lahum a'mālahum ḥabā'an manthūrā* — "We will turn to whatever deeds they did, reducing them to scattered dust." The verb *qallibnā* (We will turn, We will examine) carries both the sense of scrutiny — turning a thing over to inspect it — and transformation — turning a thing into something else. The deeds that the disbelievers performed in life, including what they considered good — acts of charity, tribal loyalty, hospitality, honoring agreements — are examined and then disintegrated. The word *ḥabā'* means the fine particles of dust that float in the air, visible only when a shaft of light passes through them. The metaphor is precise: the deeds do not merely become worthless; they become invisible, weightless, incapable of being gathered or used.

The Qur'an's treatment of deeds reduced to dust appears across multiple passages, each with its own context. In 14:18 — "The example of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes which the wind blows forcefully on a stormy day" — the image is of ashes scattered by wind. In 18:104 — "Those whose efforts are in the life of this world, while they think they are doing good — they are those who disbelieve in the verses of their Lord and in meeting Him, so their deeds are worthless" — the disqualification is tied directly to disbelief. In 25:23, the same principle applies: the deeds are nullified not because they were intrinsically evil but because the doers denied the meeting with God. Disbelief removes the foundation on which all other deeds stand.

The word *manthūrā* (scattered, dispersed) intensifies the image.
verses.24:
> ˹But˺ on that Day the residents of Paradise will have the best settlement and the finest place to rest
