**The Best Dwelling and the Finest Rest**

The verse contrasts the fate of the wicked — whose deeds are scattered into dust (25:23) — with the fate of the righteous: *aṣḥābu'l-jannati yawma'idhin khayru mustaqarrin wa khayru maqīlā* — "the residents of Paradise on that Day will have the best settlement and the finest place to rest." The word *mustaqarr* means a place of settlement, a dwelling where one is established and at rest. The word *maqīl* means a place of midday rest — the *qaylūlah*, the afternoon nap that was a fixture of Arabian life. The pairing of the two words — permanent settlement and temporary rest — covers the full range of human repose. The righteous do not merely live in Paradise; they rest in it. Every form of comfort, from the deep security of belonging to the light relief of a moment's pause, is included.

Al-Qurṭubī notes that some commentators read this verse as the direct answer to the question posed in 25:15: "Is this better, or the Garden of Eternity?" The word *khayr* (best, better) appears in both verses, creating a verbal link: what was asked about in 25:15 is confirmed in 25:24. The Garden is indeed better — not merely better than the fire but better than anything the disbelievers had in life, better than the gardens and treasures they demanded for the Prophet in 25:8, better than the earthly standards by which they measured authority and worth.

**Scattered Dust and Settled Rest: The Contrast Extended**

In 56:27-40, the description of the blessed is followed immediately by the description of the damned, with no transition or explanation. In 75:22-30, the faces of the radiant are contrasted with the faces of the darkened.

**The Delayed Answer to 25:15's Question**

Between the question in 25:15 and the answer in 25:24, the sūrah has inserted the full description of the fire (25:16-23), the angels' descent (25:25), and the sovereignty of the Most Compassionate (25:26). The answer to the question is therefore not given immediately but after the audience has absorbed the full weight of the punishment and the full scope of the Day. By the time the answer arrives — "the best dwelling and the finest rest" — the reader has earned it through the sustained experience of dread that precedes it. The delayed answer is the sūrah's way of making the promise of Paradise not merely a statement but a relief, a release from the tension that the fire descriptions built. The *maqīl* (rest) that the righteous receive is, in this reading, the rest that comes after the reader has been through the fire descriptions — the rest that the sūrah itself provides, not only to the righteous in the Hereafter but to the reader in the present, who has been absorbing the weight of the warnings for twenty verses and now receives the assurance that the outcome for the righteous is not the fire but the finest dwelling and the deepest rest. This literary architecture — tension followed by release, warning followed by promise — is one of the sūrah's most effective rhetorical strategies.

The question has implications for the nature of the Hereafter, which the Qur'an describes as a place where "they will not hear in it any ill speech — only greetings of peace" (19:62).
verses.25:
> ˹Watch for˺ the Day the heavens will burst with clouds, and the angels will be sent down in successive ranks

**The Sky Breaks Open**

The verse describes the opening scene of the Day of Judgment: *yawma tashaqqaqu's-samā'u bi-ghamāmīn* — "the Day the heavens will burst with clouds." The verb *tashaqqaqu* (to split, to burst open) appears in other Qur'anic descriptions of cosmic dissolution: in 84:1 — "When the sky is split open" — and in 82:1 — "When the sky is torn apart." The splitting of the sky is not a gradual event but a rupture, a breaking of the structure that has held the heavens in place since creation. The word *ghamām* (clouds) adds a layer of imagery: the sky does not merely open; it opens with clouds — masses of dense, heavy material that pour through the rupture. Al-Qurṭubī and others read this as a description of the physical transformation of the cosmos: the familiar sky gives way to something unprecedented, and what was above comes down.

The splitting of the heavens appears in multiple Qur'anic passages, each adding a different detail. In 42:5 — "The heavens nearly split from above them as the angels glorify their Lord" — the splitting is caused by the weight of divine glory pressing down. In 69:16 — "The sky will split open, for on that Day it will be frail" — the sky loses its structural integrity. In 78:19 — "The sky will be opened up and become gateways" — the rupture creates passages through which things descend. The verse in 25:25 combines the splitting with clouds and then adds the descent of the angels, making the rupture the opening act of a larger drama: the cosmos breaks, and through the break come the agents of judgment.

**The Angels in Successive Ranks**

The descent of the angels is mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an in connection with the Day of Judgment. In 2:210 — "Do they wait until Allah and the angels come to them in the shadows of clouds?" — the descent is framed as something the disbelievers should anticipate. In 89:22 — "And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank" — the descent is described with the same sense of overwhelming presence. In 6:158 — "The Day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith unless it had believed before" — the arrival of the signs marks the end of the period in which belief is possible. The angels in 25:25 are part of this sequence: their descent is not a sign to encourage faith but a declaration that faith's opportunity has ended.

**The Angels as Agents of Judgment**

The descent of the angels in successive ranks (*munzalatan*) carries a specific function in the Qur'anic the doctrine of the Last Day that goes beyond the spectacular imagery. They carry the throne (69:17), they drive the sinners to Hell (74:30-31), they greet the righteous at the gates of Paradise (13:23-24), and they bear witness against the disbelievers (41:22). Their descent through the broken sky in 25:25 is therefore not a passive event but an active deployment — a cosmic army arriving for a specific mission. The effect on the disbelievers — described in 25:22 as the cry of "Keep away!" — is the natural response to a force of this magnitude. The disbelievers, who demanded to see the angels in 25:21 as a condition for belief, now face the angels as a condition for judgment, and the difference between the two conditions is the difference between an invitation and a sentence.
verses.26:
> True authority on that Day will belong ˹only˺ to the Most Compassionate. And it will be a hard day for the disbelievers

**The Only Sovereignty That Remains**

The verse declares that on the Day described in 25:25 — the sky splitting, the angels descending in ranks — the *mulk* (sovereignty, dominion) will belong to the Most Compassionate alone. The phrase *al-mulku yawma'idhin al-ḥaqqu lil-Raḥmān* places the article *al-ḥaqq* (the true, the real) before God's name, making the statement not merely that God will have sovereignty but that His sovereignty is the only real sovereignty — the only dominion that is true, legitimate, and ultimate. Every other claim to authority — every king, every empire, every tribal chief, every political system — is revealed on that Day as a temporary arrangement, a borrowed power that was never truly held.

The same declaration appears in other Qur'anic passages with the same force. In 18:44 — "There the authority belongs entirely to Allah, the True" — the context is a description of the destruction of a civilization, after which only God's dominion remains. In 40:16 — "The Day they come forth, nothing about them will be concealed from Allah. To whom belongs the sovereignty this Day? To Allah, the One, the All-Dominant" — the question is posed rhetorically, and the answer is stated before the audience can respond. In 25:26, the declaration follows the cosmic disruption of 25:25: the sky has broken, the angels have descended, and in the midst of that upheaval, the only thing that is stable, the only thing that is real, is the dominion of the Most Compassionate.

**Raḥmān: The Name That Implies Mercy in the Midst of Judgment**

The sūrah's use of *al-Raḥmān* connects to its earlier appearances. In 25:60, the disbelievers will be asked to prostrate to the Most Compassionate and will refuse. In 25:63-76, the servants of the Most Compassionate are described in detail. The name *al-Raḥmān* is thus a thread running through the sūrah, connecting the judgment of the disbelievers to the character of the God they rejected.

**Yawmun ʿalā'l-kāfirīna ʿasīr: The Day's Hardness**

The phrase *yawmun ʿalā'l-kāfirīna ʿasīr* — "a hard day for the disbelievers" — uses the word *ʿasīr* (difficult, hard, severe). The same word appears in 73:5 — "We will soon cast upon you a heavy word" — where it describes the weight of the Qur'anic revelation itself. In 25:26, the weight belongs to the Day: it presses down on the disbelievers with a force they cannot resist. The hardness is not abstract; it is experienced. The disbelievers will feel the weight of the Day in their bodies, their minds, and their spirits, and the weight corresponds to the gravity of what they denied. They denied the sovereignty of the Most Compassionate; the Day shows that sovereignty in the most visible and inescapable way possible.

The phrase also serves as a bridge to the verses that follow. In 25:27, the wrongdoer will bite his nails in regret and wish he had followed the Messenger. The hardness of the Day produces that regret — not mere sorrow but the kind of all-consuming remorse that makes a person destroy their own hands in grief. The hardness is not a single event but a condition, a state of being that persists throughout the Day and produces ever-deeper consequences as it unfolds.
verses.27:
> And ˹beware of˺ the Day the wrongdoer will bite his nails ˹in regret˺ and say, “Oh! I wish I had followed the Way along with the Messenger

**The Gesture of Self-Destruction**

The verse describes the wrongdoer's response to the Day declared in 25:26: *yawma yaʿaddu'ẓ-ẓālimu ʿalā yadayhi* — "the Day the wrongdoer will bite his hands." The verb *yaʿaddu* means to bite, and the object is *yadayhi* — his two hands. The image is visceral: a person so consumed by regret that they attack their own body, biting their hands as though the hands were responsible for what they did. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the gesture is an expression of extreme grief in Arabian culture — the biting of the hands is a sign of helplessness, of the inability to undo what has been done, of rage directed inward because there is nowhere else to direct it.

The phrase *naḍiman ʿalā mā farrata fī'l-amr* — "in regret over what he neglected in the matter" — specifies the cause. The word *farrata* means to neglect, to let slip, to waste an opportunity.

**"I Wish I Had Taken a Way With the Messenger"**

The wrongdoer's wish — *yā laytanī ittakhadhtu maʿa'r-rasūli sabīlā* — uses the word *sabīl* (way, path), the same word that appeared in 25:9 to describe what the disbelievers could not find. In 25:9, they went so far astray that they "could not find the way"; in 25:27, the wrongdoer wishes he had taken the way with the Messenger. The verbal echo connects the two passages: the inability to find the way in life becomes the desperate wish for the way in death. The *sabīl* that was available — that was offered, that was walked by the Prophet and his companions — is now the thing the wrongdoer most desires and cannot have.

The phrase *maʿa'r-rasūli* ("with the Messenger") is significant. The wrongdoer does not wish he had followed the way in general; he wishes he had followed it specifically alongside the Messenger. The Prophet ﷺ was the embodiment of the path — the living example of what the Criterion (25:1) looked like in practice — and to walk with him would have been to walk the way. The wish is not for abstract faith but for companionship with the one who showed faith. The wrongdoer's regret is therefore not merely theological but personal: he misses the person he rejected.

**The Transition to Blaming the Friend**

Verse 25:27 ends with the wrongdoer's self-reproach, and 25:28 will shift the blame to the friend who led him astray. The transition is psychologically precise. The first response to catastrophic regret is self-blame: "I wish I had followed." The second response, when self-blame becomes unbearable, is to find someone else to blame: "I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a friend." The movement from self-accusation to other-accusation is the human response to irreversible failure. The Qur'an records both stages without choosing between them. The wrongdoer is responsible for his own choices, and the friend who influenced him is also responsible. The Day of Judgment will hold each accountable for their own part, but the wrongdoer, standing in the moment of regret, has not yet arrived at that distinction. He is still in the rawness of loss, and the rawness expresses itself as alternating waves of self-blame and blame of others.
verses.28:
> Woe to me! I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a close friend

**So-and-So: The Unnamed Friend**

The verse uses *fulānan* — "so-and-so" — to refer to the friend, leaving the identity unnamed. Al-Qurṭubī records that some commentators tie these verses to a specific historical incident — a man of Madinah who was led away from Islam by a companion — but the majority position, supported by al-Rāzī, is that the verses are general. The use of *fulānan* makes the warning universal: every person who has a close friend should consider whether that friendship is leading them toward the Messenger or away from him.

**The Companion Who Replaced the Reminder**

Verse 25:29 will explain what the friend did: he led the wrongdoer away from the Reminder after it had reached him. The placement of 25:28 before 25:29 is the sūrah's way of building the wrongdoer's confession in stages. First, self-blame (25:27): I wish I had followed the Messenger. Then, other-blame (25:28): I wish I had not taken this friend. Then, diagnosis (25:29): the friend led me astray from the Reminder. The sequence moves from regret to accusation to explanation, and each stage adds a layer of understanding. The wrongdoer is not only suffering; he is analyzing his own failure, tracing it from its symptom (not following the Messenger) to its cause (the companion who replaced the Messenger's guidance with something else).

**The Weight of Companionship in the Qur'an**

The Qur'an assigns enormous moral weight to the choice of companions. In 25:27-28, the wrongdoer traces his ruin to a single relationship — the *khalīl* (intimate friend) who led him astray. This is not an isolated theme; it runs through the Qur'an's moral teaching. In 18:28 — "And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance" — the Prophet is instructed to choose his companions from among the devoted. In 43:67 — "Close friends on that Day will be foes to one another, except for the God-conscious" — the dissolution of worldly friendships on the Day of Judgment is described. In 70:10-11 — "And no intimate friend will ask about his intimate friend, though they will be shown each other" — the bonds that seemed permanent in life prove to be temporary in death. The wrongdoer's wish in 25:28 — "I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a close friend" — is the negative expression of this teaching. The positive expression is the Qur'an's instruction to choose companions who draw one toward God rather than away from Him. The choice of a *khalīl* is not a social decision but a moral one, and the consequences of that choice extend beyond this life into the Day when friends become strangers and strangers become neighbors in the fire or the garden. The theological weight of companionship in the Qur’an is not only moral but cosmological: the friends one chooses shape the soul’s orientation, and the soul’s orientation determines its destination. The wrongdoer’s khalīl did not merely distract him from the Reminder; the khalīl replaced the Reminder as the wrongdoer’s primary source of guidance. The friend’s voice became more authoritative than God’s voice, and the friend’s opinion became more compelling than God’s revelation. This replacement is the mechanism of misguidance: it is not the addition of falsehood but the substitution of one authority for another.
verses.29:
> It was he who truly made me stray from the Reminder after it had reached me.” And Satan has always betrayed humanity

**Satan as the Archetype of Betrayal**

The verse closes with a general statement: *wa kāna's-shayṭānu lil-insāni khaḍūlā* — "And Satan has always betrayed humanity." The word *khaḍūl* means one who betrays, abandons, lets down. Satan's defining characteristic, in the Qur'anic portrayal, is not cruelty but desertion: he tempts, he leads astray, and then he abandons those who followed him. In 14:22 — "Satan will say when the matter is decided, 'Allah gave you a truthful promise, and I gave you a promise and broke it. I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me'" — Satan confesses that he was never a true ally. He was a voice, a suggestion, an influence — and when the consequences arrive, he disowns his followers completely.

The word *khaḍūl* applies to both Satan and to the human friend the wrongdoer blamed in 25:28. The friend who led him astray was a *shayṭān* in the extended sense the Qur'an allows: *shayṭān* (Satan) is not only the proper name of Iblīs but a category that includes any being — human or jinn — who leads others away from the truth. In 6:112 — "We have made for every prophet enemies — satans from among mankind and jinn, who inspire each other with flowery discourse to deceive" — the word *shayāṭīn* (satans) is applied to human beings who act as Satan's agents. The wrongdoer's friend in 25:28 is one such agent, and the closing statement of 25:29 names the pattern: Satan betrays, and those who serve Satan's purpose betray in the same way. The friend who led the wrongdoer astray will not stand with him on the Day of Judgment; like Satan, the friend will have abandoned his companion to face the consequences alone.

**The Reminder That Was Abandoned**

The word *dhikr* (Reminder) in 25:29 refers to the Quran itself — one of whose names is *al-dhikr* (the Reminder) — and to the broader act of remembering God. The wrongdoer's confession that his friend led him away from the Reminder "after it had reached me" specifies a sequence: the Reminder arrived first, the friend intervened second. This sequence is crucial because it establishes that the wrongdoer had access to the truth before the friend's influence took hold. The Reminder was not abstract or distant; it had *reached* him — *jā'anī* — and was available for acceptance. The mechanism is one the Qur'an describes elsewhere: "Satan promises them and arouses desire in them, but Satan does not promise them except delusion" (4:120). The friend served as a *shayṭān* — a tempter, an agent of misguidance — and the temptation succeeded because the wrongdoer valued the friend's companionship more than the Reminder's truth. The verse's closing declaration — "Satan has always been a betrayer of humanity" — names the archetype and warns that the pattern will repeat: every person who chooses a human companion over divine guidance will find, on the Day of Judgment, that the companion was a satan in disguise. The betrayal was built into the relationship from the start.
verses.30:
> The Messenger has cried, “O my Lord! My people have indeed received this Quran with neglect.”

**The Prophet's Complaint to God**

The verse shifts from the wrongdoer's confession to the Prophet's complaint: *wa qāla'r-rasūlu yā Rabbi inna qawmī ittakhadhū hādhā'l-qur'āna mahjūrā* — "And the Messenger said, 'O my Lord, my people have indeed taken this Quran as something neglected.'" The word *mahjūr* means neglected, abandoned, treated as something to be avoided. It is the same root as *ḥijr* (barrier, forbidden zone) in 25:22, where the disbelievers cried "Keep away! A forbidden barrier!" The verbal echo connects the two passages: the disbelievers kept away from the Quran, and the Prophet now reports to God that his people have treated the revelation as something from which to maintain distance.

Al-Rāzī records both readings and notes that the present tense *ittakhadhū* ("they have taken") is compatible with either time frame.

**The Prophet's Grief and the Limits of His Responsibility**

The verse reveals the emotional reality of prophethood. The Prophet ﷺ did not deliver the Quran with detachment; he delivered it with the full weight of his concern for his people. The complaint — "my people have received this Quran with neglect" — is not a report of facts; it is a cry of grief. The word *yā Rabbi* ("O my Lord") is an address of intimacy, the appeal of a servant to his master, a child to his parent. The Prophet is not asking for punishment or for vindication; he is expressing the pain of watching the thing he loves most — the revelation — be treated with contempt by the people he loves most — his community.

The Qur'an records this complaint without judgment. It does not rebuke the Prophet for expressing his grief, nor does it tell him to be more patient. The recording itself is an act of validation: the Prophet's grief is real, it is appropriate, and it is heard by God. The same dynamic appears in 5:41 — "O Messenger, do not be grieved by those who race toward disbelief" — where the divine response acknowledges the Prophet's emotional state without suppressing it. Prophethood in the Qur'an is not stoic; it is human, and the human cost of delivering a message that is rejected is the grief that 25:30 makes visible.

**The Sūrah's Voice: From Disbelievers to Prophet**

The sūrah has moved through several voices: the disbelievers speak in 25:4-8 and 25:21, the wrongdoer speaks in 25:27-29, and now the Prophet speaks in 25:30. Each voice reveals a different dimension of the same conflict. The disbelievers' voice reveals their objections; the wrongdoer's voice reveals their consequences; the Prophet's voice reveals the human cost. The sūrah's structure is not linear but polyphonic — multiple speakers, multiple perspectives, all addressing the same central question: what happens when the truth is offered and refused? The Prophet's cry in 25:30 is the heart of the sūrah's emotional argument: the Quran was not merely rejected; it was neglected, abandoned, treated as though it did not exist. And the one who delivered it is left to bear the weight of that neglect alone.
verses.31:
> Similarly, We made enemies for every prophet from among the wicked, but sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and Helper

**The Prophetic Pattern of Opposition**

The verse answers the Prophet's grief from 25:30 with a statement of historical fact: *wa kathālika jaʿalnā li-kulli nabiyyin ʿaduwwan min al-mujrimīn* — "Similarly, We have made for every prophet enemies from among the wicked." The word *kathālika* ("similarly," "in the same way") places the Prophet Muhammad's experience inside an universal pattern. His rejection is not unique; every prophet before him faced enemies drawn from the same category of people — *al-mujrimīn*, the sinners, the criminals, those who have placed themselves in the wrong. The comfort is not that the suffering is less but that it is shared: the Prophet stands in a line of messengers who were all opposed by the same kind of people for the same kind of reasons.

The verse that most closely parallels this one is 6:112 — "Similarly, We have made for every prophet enemies — satans from among mankind and jinn, who inspire each other with flowery discourse to deceive." That verse specifies the mechanism: the enemies are *shayāṭīn* (satans), both human and non-human, who work together to oppose the prophetic message. In 25:31, the mechanism is left unstated, but the category is the same: the enemies come from among the criminals, the people whose way of life is threatened by the message. The prophetic mission, by its nature, disrupts existing power structures, and those who benefit from the disruption's absence will oppose the messenger. The opposition is not a sign of the message's failure but of its relevance: a message that threatens no one changes nothing.

**God's Sufficiency as Guide and Helper**

The second half of the verse — *wa kafā bi-Rabbika hādiyan wa naṣīrān* — responds to the Prophet's complaint with a direct assurance: your Lord is enough as a Guide and a Helper. The word *kafā* (enough, enough) appears in similar contexts across the Qur'an. In 3:173 — "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs" — the word is spoken by the believers when they face an army larger than their own. In 4:79 — "Whatever good comes to you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself" — the sufficiency of God is paired with the reality of human responsibility. In 25:31, the sufficiency addresses the Prophet's specific need: he has complained that his people neglect the Quran, and God responds that the Prophet does not need their acceptance. God is enough — as a Guide who directs the message to those who will receive it, and as a Helper who protects the messenger from those who reject it.

**The Subsequent Catalogue of Prophetic Enemies**

The commentators note that the verses following 25:31 — the mention of Moses and Aaron (25:35-36), Noah (25:37), ʿĀd and Thamūd (25:38), and the people of Lot (25:40) — function as an extended commentary on the principle stated in 25:31. Each of these prophets faced enemies from among the criminals, and each of those enemies was ultimately destroyed. The catalogue serves two purposes: it confirms the Prophet Muhammad's experience as part of a larger pattern, and it warns the disbelievers of Makkah that the pattern includes not only opposition but consequence. The prophets' enemies were not vindicated by history; they were destroyed by God. The disbelievers of Makkah are standing in the same position as the enemies of Noah, Moses, and Lot, and the verse invites them to consider whether they want to share that position's outcome.
verses.32:
> The disbelievers say, “If only the Quran had been sent down to him all at once!” ˹We have sent it˺ as such ˹in stages˺ so We may reassure your heart with it. And We have revealed it at a deliberate pace

The disbelievers return with another objection, recorded in their own words: *wa qāla'lladhīna kafarū law-lā nuzzila ʿalayhi'l-qur'ānu jumlatan wāḥidatan* — "If only the Quran had been sent down to him all at once!" The demand echoes their earlier objections in 25:4-8: they have tried to explain the Quran as fabrication, as borrowed tales, as bewitchment. Now they try a new angle — it should have come all at once, like a book, like a completed text delivered in a single package.

**The Divine Reason: Reassurance of the Heart**

The divine response — *li-nuthabbita bihi fu'ādaka wa rattalnāhu tartīlā* — names a single purpose for the gradual revelation: "so We may reassure your heart with it." The word *nuthabbita* (to make firm, to establish, to reassure) is the same word used in 11:120 — "All that We relate to you of the stories of the messengers is that by which We make firm your heart." The Quran's stories, laws. Urgings were not delivered to a finished prophet; they were delivered to a growing one. The piecemeal nature of the revelation allowed the Prophet ﷺ to absorb, internalize, and live each part before the next arrived. A single overwhelming delivery would have been a burden; the gradual delivery was a support.

**Tartīlā: The Pace of Deliberate Recitation**

The final word — *wa rattalnāhu tartīlā* — is translated as "We have revealed it at a deliberate pace," but the Arabic carries additional layers. *Tartīl* means measured, ordered, arranged in proper sequence. The same word is used in 73:4 — "And recite the Quran in a measured tone" — where it describes the Prophet's own recitation. The connection between the two verses reveals a correspondence: the revelation came in a measured way so that it could be received and recited in a measured way. The pace of revelation shaped the pace of worship, of memorization, of communal life. The piecemeal delivery was not a deficiency but a design, and the design produced a community that lived with the Quran as it arrived, absorbing it verse by verse, day by day, year by year.

The disbelievers' demand for a single delivery would have eliminated this gradual immersion. A book delivered all at once is read once and shelved; a revelation that arrives over twenty-three years is lived. The difference is between a text and a companion, and the Quran, as the sūrah presents it, was always intended to be the latter.
verses.33:
> Whenever they bring you an argument, We come to you with the right refutation and the best explanation

**The Divine Guarantee of Refutation**

The verse is addressed to the Prophet with a promise: *wa lā ya'tūnaka bi-mathalin illā ji'nāka bi'l-ḥaqqi wa aḥsana tafsīrā* — "And they do not bring you any argument but that We come to you with the truth and a better explanation." The word *mathal* (parable, argument, comparison) refers to the objections the disbelievers raised throughout the sūrah — the charges of fabrication (25:4), borrowing (25:5), bewitchment (25:8), and the demands for material signs (25:7-8). Each of these was a *mathal*, a rhetorical construction designed to discredit the Prophet. The promise is that every such construction will be met with *al-ḥaqq* (the truth) and *aḥsana tafsīrā* (the best explanation).

The word *tafsīr* is significant because it later became the technical term for Qur'anic exegesis. In 25:33, it refers to God's own explanation of the truth — not human commentary but divine clarification. The explanation is always better (*aḥsana*) than the argument it answers, because it comes from a higher source and addresses a deeper level. The disbelievers' arguments operate on the surface — accusation, mockery, comparison. God's explanations operate at the level of reality — what is true, what is real, what will last. The asymmetry is permanent: no argument the disbelievers construct can exceed the explanation God provides, because the explanations come from the One who knows everything (25:6: "the One Who knows the secrets of the heavens and the earth").

**The Sūrah's Own Demonstration of This Promise**

The verse can be read as a description of the sūrah's own structure. The sūrah opens with the disbelievers' objections (25:4-8), and each objection is answered by the verses that follow. The charge of fabrication is answered by the declaration of divine origin (25:6). The demand for material signs is answered by the promise of Paradise (25:10). The denial of the Hour is answered by the description of the fire and the garden (25:11-16). The demand for visible angels is answered by the description of the angels' descent on the Day of Judgment (25:22, 25:25). The sūrah itself is the demonstration of the principle 25:33 states: every argument is met with a better explanation, and the explanations accumulate until the case is complete.
verses.34:
> Those who will be dragged into Hell on their faces will be in the worst place, and are ˹now˺ farthest from the ˹Right˺ Way

**The Face as the Instrument of Punishment**

The verse describes the manner of entry into Hell: *alladhīna yuḥsharūna ʿalā wujūhim ilā jahannam* — "those who will be gathered upon their faces into Hell." The image is one of total degradation: human beings dragged to punishment not on their feet, not walking, not even carried, but on their faces. The face in every culture is the seat of identity, dignity, and recognition. To be dragged on the face is to have every form of dignity removed — the person cannot see where they are going, cannot choose their direction, cannot present themselves as anything other than what they are: a creature in the hands of a power that has decided their destination.

The same image appears in other Qur'anic Last-Day passages. In 17:97 — "We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection, fallen on their faces, blind, mute, and deaf" — the loss of faculties (sight, speech, hearing) accompanies the loss of posture. In 54:48 — "The Day they are dragged into the Fire on their faces" — the verb *yusḥarūna* (dragged) emphasizes the force involved. In 8:50 — "If only you could see when the angels take the souls of the disbelievers, striking their faces and their backs" — the face is the target of the angels' blows. The Qur'an's consistent association of the face with the punishment of the disbelievers is not incidental: it is the ultimate reversal of the human tendency to present the face — to show dignity, to demand respect, to maintain appearance. The face that was used to project pride in life is used to absorb humiliation in death.

**Ashqa: The Worst Position**

The word *aḍallu sabīlā* — "farthest from the Way" — echoes the sūrah's recurring use of *sabīl* (way, path) to describe guidance. In 25:9, the disbelievers "could not find the way." In 25:27, the wrongdoer wishes he "had taken a way with the Messenger." In 25:34, the final position of the disbelievers is defined by their distance from the Way. The sūrah tracks the concept of *sabīl* from inability (25:9) to regret (25:27) to final distance (25:34), and the trajectory is one of increasing loss. The Way was available at every point; the disbelievers moved further from it at every point; and the final position — dragged into Hell on their faces — is the terminus of that movement.

**The Face as the Seat of Identity and Dignity**

The Qur'an's consistent association of the face with the punishment of the disbelievers and with the reward of the righteous creates a theological vocabulary centered on the human face. In 80:38-39 — "Faces on that Day will be radiant, laughing, rejoicing" — the righteous are described through their faces. In 88:2-3 — "Some faces on that Day will be humbled, exhausted and weary" — the disbelievers are described the same way. The face is the visible seat of the self — the place where identity, emotion, and dignity are displayed — and the Qur'an uses it as the primary marker of a person's spiritual state. In 25:34, the face is pressed into the ground, dragged toward Hell, and the degradation is total because the face is the last thing a person surrenders. The punishment in 25:34 crosses that frontier: the face is not only humiliated but used as the instrument of transport, and the person is reduced to the physical surface of their body. The contrast with the radiant faces of the righteous (80:38) is the sūrah's unstated comparison: what the righteous receive in beauty, the disbelievers receive in degradation, and the organ of both is the same.
verses.35:
> We certainly gave Moses the Book and appointed his brother Aaron as his helper

**The Introduction of Moses Into the Sūrah's Argument**

The verse marks a shift in the sūrah's method. Since 25:4, the text has been responding to the disbelievers' objections directly — answering their charges, describing their punishment, recording their regret. Beginning with 25:35, the sūrah introduces a catalogue of earlier prophets and the fates of their opponents. Moses is mentioned first, with a specific detail: God gave him the Book (*al-kitāb*) and appointed his brother Aaron (*Hārūn*) as his helper (*wazīr*).

The word *wazīr* (helper, minister) is the same word used in modern Arabic for a government minister, and its Qur'anic usage establishes the concept: a *wazīr* is one who bears the burden alongside the leader. In 20:29-32, Moses asks God to "appoint for me a minister from my family, Aaron my brother. Strengthen me through him and let him share my task." The request and the granting are recorded in 25:35 without elaboration, because the sūrah's purpose is not to retell the story but to establish the pattern: every prophet had help, and every prophet's help came from God.

**The Book as a Criterion**

The phrase *ātaynā Mūsā'l-kitāb* — "We gave Moses the Book" — refers to the Torah, which the Qur'an elsewhere calls *al-Furqān* (the Criterion). In 2:53 — "And when We gave Moses the Scripture and the Criterion, that you might be guided" — the Torah is given the same title as this sūrah. In 21:48 — "We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder for the God-conscious" — the Criterion is paired with light and reminder. The connection is significant: Moses received the Criterion, and Muhammad ﷺ received the Criterion, and the two revelations serve the same function — to distinguish truth from falsehood, to provide guidance, to separate the believers from the disbelievers. The mention of Moses' Book in 25:35 is thus not merely historical; it is structural. The Criterion that names this sūrah is the same kind of revelation that Moses received, and the opposition it provokes is the same kind of opposition.

**The Verse's Role in the Prophetic Catalogue**

Verses 25:35-40 form a catalogue of prophets and the destruction of their enemies. Moses and Aaron are mentioned in 25:35-36, Noah in 25:37, ʿĀd and Thamūd and the people of the Water-pit in 25:38-39, and the people of Lot in 25:40. The catalogue answers the statement of 25:31 — "We have made enemies for every prophet from among the wicked" — by providing specific examples. Each example follows the same pattern: a prophet was sent, the people rejected him, and God destroyed the rejecters. The pattern is the sūrah's final argument against the disbelievers of Makkah: the history of prophetic opposition is also a history of prophetic vindication. The prophets were opposed, but the prophets survived; the enemies were powerful, but the enemies were destroyed. The disbelievers of Makkah are invited to place themselves in this history and decide which role they are playing.

The mention of Aaron as Moses' helper also serves the Prophet Muhammad indirectly. The disbelievers mocked the Prophet for being an ordinary man (25:7); Moses, the greatest prophet in the Qur'an's telling, was also an ordinary man who needed a helper. The fact that God gave Moses a helper does not diminish Moses; it shows that prophetic missions are carried out by human beings within human limitations, supported by God through human means. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did not have a human helper in the same sense — he was both the messenger and the community builder — but the principle is the same: the mission does not require the absence of human need; it requires the presence of divine support.

Moses needed Aaron to speak on his behalf (20:29-34: "My brother Aaron is more eloquent than me, so send him with me as a helper"); Muhammad needed the companions to memorize, practice, and transmit the Quran.
verses.36:
> We had ordered ˹them˺, “Go to the people who would deny Our signs.” Then We annihilated the deniers entirely

**The Command and Its Execution**

The verse compresses the essential structure of the prophetic mission into a single sentence: a command, an audience, and a consequence. *Fa-qulnā'dhhabā ilā'l-qawmi'lladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā* — "So We said, 'Go to the people who denied Our signs.'" The command is given in the dual form, addressed to Moses and Aaron together, which is consistent with the Qur'anic account in 20:42 and 26:12-16 where both are commissioned. The people in question are the Egyptians under Pharaoh, who rejected the evidentiary signs (*āyāt*) that Moses brought — the staff, the leprous hand, the plagues, the parting of the sea.

In 25:36, it refers to the miraculous signs, but the sūrah's reader has been trained by this point to hear the echo: the disbelievers of Makkah have also denied the signs — the signs of the Quran's divine origin, the signs in creation, the signs in the fate of earlier nations.

**Dammarnā: The Word for Complete Destruction**

The verse's final clause — *fa-dammarnāhum tadbīrān* — "Then We destroyed them completely" — uses the verb *dammara*, which means to annihilate, to destroy utterly, to bring to total ruin. The same verb appears in 7:137, 17:16, 26:172, 27:51, 37:136, and 47:10, each time describing God's complete destruction of a people who rejected His messenger. The word *tadbīr* intensifies it: the destruction was thorough, systematic, and total. Nothing was left. The Egyptians who denied Moses' signs were not merely defeated; they were erased.

Al-Qurṭubī notes the connection between the command to "go to" the deniers and the destruction that followed. The prophets did not destroy their enemies; God did. The prophets' role was to deliver the message and to stand their ground; the consequence was God's alone. This division of labor is consistent across the Qur'an's prophetic narratives: the messenger warns, the people reject, and God executes the judgment. The prophets are not warriors; they are witnesses. Their presence among the people is the final warning, and when the warning is rejected, the consequence follows — not from the messenger's hand but from God's.

**The Dual Form and Its Implication**

This detail, though grammatically minor, carries a narrative significance that al-Qurṭubī highlights. In some Qur'anic passages, the command to confront Pharaoh is addressed to Moses alone (20:24; 26:16); in others, it is addressed to both brothers (20:42; 26:12-16). The variation reflects the evolving composition of the prophetic mission: Moses was the primary messenger, and Aaron was appointed as his helper after Moses requested assistance. The dual form in 25:36 records the state of the mission after the appointment — both brothers, working together, confronting the deniers. The phrase "the people who denied Our signs" identifies the target not by ethnicity (the Egyptians) but by behavior (denial of signs). The same behavior is what defines the disbelievers of Makkah, and the sūrah's use of the behavioral description rather than the ethnic name makes the parallel explicit. The deniers of Moses' signs and the deniers of Muhammad's signs are the same kind of people, distinguished by the same act — the refusal to recognize the divine origin of the evidence presented to them. The destruction that followed the denial in Moses' case is the warning for Muhammad's case, and the warning is the reason the story is told.
verses.37:
> And when the people of Noah rejected the messengers, We drowned them, making them an example to humanity. And We have prepared a painful punishment for the wrongdoers

**Noah: The First and the Universal**

The verse introduces Noah into the catalogue with a detail that goes beyond the Moses episode: the people of Noah rejected not one messenger but "the messengers" (*al-mursalīn*), in the plural. This has puzzled some commentators, since Noah is typically understood as the first messenger in the Qur'anic narrative. Al-Qurṭubī explains that the plural is used because rejecting one messenger is equivalent to rejecting all of them — the message is one, the source is one, and the principle of rejection is universal. Others hold that Noah's people rejected the messengers in the sense that they rejected the principle of messengership itself, refusing to accept that God sends anyone to guide humanity.

Noah occupies an unique position in the Qur'anic narrative as the first prophet to be sent to a community that had fallen into idolatry (7:59). The mention of Noah in 25:37 invokes this template and applies it to the Prophet Muhammad's situation: the disbelievers of Makkah are standing in the position of Noah's people, and the consequence is the same.

**Drowning as a Sign for Humanity**

This use of historical destruction as a sign appears throughout the Qur'an. In 15:79 — "So We took retribution from them, and both are on a clear highway" — the ruins of the destroyed cities are situated on a road that travelers pass. In 29:40 — "We seized each people for their sin" — the punishment is linked to specific places that still exist. The sūrah itself will use this device in 25:40, where the disbelievers are reminded that they have passed by the ruins of Sodom. The pattern is consistent: God destroys, preserves the ruins, and invites the living to reflect on what the ruins mean. The people of Noah are the first entry in this catalogue of ruins, and the lesson they teach is the same lesson every entry teaches: rejection has consequences, and the consequences are visible to anyone willing to look.

**The Recurring Phrase: A Painful Punishment for the Wrongdoers**

The verse ends with *wa aʿtadnā li'ẓ-ẓālimīna ʿadhāban alīmā* — "And We have prepared a painful punishment for the wrongdoers." This phrase, or close variants of it, appears multiple times in the sūrah and across the Qur'an as a refrain. Its repetition serves a dual purpose: for the prophets' enemies of the past, it confirms the outcome — they were punished; for the disbelievers of the present, it warns of the same outcome approaching. The word *aʿtadnā* (We have prepared) uses the past tense, as in 25:11, giving the punishment the quality of readiness. It is not being assembled; it exists, waiting for those who join the ranks of the wrongdoers by repeating the pattern the catalogue describes.
verses.38:
> Also ˹We destroyed˺ ’Ȃd, Thamûd, and the people of the Water-pit, as well as many peoples in between

**The Arab Catastrophes: Destructions Within Living Memory**

The verse names three destroyed peoples — ʿĀd, Thamūd, and the people of the Water-pit (*al-Rass*) — and adds "many peoples in between." The first two are central to the Qur'an's prophetic geography because their ruins were visible in the Arabian Peninsula. The ʿĀd, the people of the prophet Hūd, lived in the region of al-Aḥqāf in southern Arabia and were destroyed by a devastating wind (41:16; 69:6-7; 89:6-7). The Thamūd, the people of the prophet Ṣāliḥ, lived in the region of al-Ḥijr (modern Mada'in Ṣāliḥ in northwestern Saudi Arabia) and were destroyed by an earthquake and a blast (7:78; 11:67; 15:80-83). Both peoples left physical ruins that the Quraysh knew — the Thamūd's carved rock dwellings were visible on the trade routes to Syria — and the Qur'an repeatedly invites its audience to visit these ruins and learn from them (15:84; 29:38; 46:25).

The mention of these peoples in 25:38 is not only historical; it is geographic. The disbelievers of Makkah lived in a landscape scarred by divine punishment. The ruins of the ʿĀd and the Thamūd were not distant legends; they were features of the physical world the Quraysh moved through. The sūrah's catalogue of destroyed peoples is a map of the Arabian Peninsula drawn in consequence: north, the ruins of Thamūd; south, the ruins of ʿĀd; and the disbelievers sit in the middle, on the same land, under the same sky, making the same choices.

**Al-Rass: The People of the Water-Pit**

The identity of the people of al-Rass is uncertain, and the commentators acknowledge this directly. Al-Rāzī lists several possibilities: some scholars say the name refers to a geographical location, others that it refers to the act of throwing their prophet into a well or pit (*rass* can mean "well" or "pit"). The people of al-Rass are also mentioned in 50:12 alongside the ʿĀd, Pharaoh, and the brethren of Lot, suggesting they were a well-known destroyed community in the Qur'anic audience's frame of reference. The Qur'an does not elaborate on their story, and the commentators who try identification acknowledge that the details are not ascertainable. What is certain is the pattern: a prophet was sent, the people rejected him, and they were destroyed. The identity of the prophet and the exact location are less important than the principle.

**"Many Peoples in Between"**

The phrase *wa quranan bayna dhālika kathīrān* — "and many peoples in between" — expands the catalogue beyond the named examples. The destruction of communities that rejected their prophets was not limited to a few dramatic cases; it was a recurring feature of human history. The word *quran* (generations, peoples) suggests that entire generations were erased — not just individuals but communities, cultures, civilizations. The phrase "in between" implies that the destructions were distributed across geography and time, covering the whole of the inhabited world. The catalogue is therefore not exhaustive but representative: the named examples are the ones the audience would recognize, and the unnamed ones are the ones that history has forgotten but God has not.

The disbelievers of Makkah might be tempted to think that the destruction of the ʿĀd and the Thamūd was exceptional — a few extreme cases that do not apply to them. The phrase "many peoples in between" closes that escape: the destruction was not exceptional but normal.
verses.39:
> For each We set forth ˹various˺ lessons, and We ultimately destroyed each

**The Word Amthāl: Parables as Warnings**

The word *amthāl* in 25:39 does not mean "parables" in the literary sense — short stories with moral lessons — but something broader: examples, comparisons, warnings drawn from experience. Al-Ṭabarī glosses the word as *ibrar wa ḥujaj* — "admonitions and proofs." Each destroyed community was given not only a prophet but also the means to understand the prophet's message: signs in nature, signs in their own history, signs in the fate of communities that had gone before them. The word *amthāl* encompasses all of these. God did not simply send a messenger and wait; He provided the evidence that the messenger's claim was true, and He provided it in forms the audience could recognize.

**The Formula of Warning and Destruction**

Verse 25:39 distills the sūrah's prophetic catalogue to its essential formula: God provided lessons (*amthāl*), and God destroyed (*tabbīr*). The formula has two verbs and no middle ground — there is no third option between receiving the lessons and being destroyed. This binary structure is the sūrah's most severe theological claim: there is no path that avoids both outcomes. The lessons are the prophets, the signs, the warnings, and the historical evidence of prior destructions. A person who receives these lessons and responds to them moves toward the Garden described in 25:15-16 and 25:24. The word *amthāl* (lessons, parables) encompasses every form of divine communication: the Quran's verses, the prophets' words, the signs in creation, and the ruins of destroyed communities. All of these are *amthāl* — comparisons, examples, demonstrations — designed to teach, warn, and persuade. The destruction that follows their refusal is not arbitrary but logical: a community that rejects every form of guidance has removed itself from the possibility of guidance, and the destruction is the consequence of that removal. The formula in 25:39 is the sūrah's way of saying: the evidence was given, the choice was made, and the outcome was determined by the choice. The word mathal (parable, lesson) in 25:39 connects this verse to 25:33, where the same word appears in the context of the disbelievers’ arguments. In 25:33, the mathal is the disbelievers’ rhetorical challenge; in 25:39, the amthāl are God’s warnings to the destroyed communities. The disbelievers construct amthāl to discredit the Prophet; God constructs amthāl to warn the disbelievers. The symmetry is deliberate: the sūrah is showing that the rhetorical tools the disbelievers use against the Prophet are the same tools God has used against every previous generation of rejecters.

The verse performs a compression: it takes the multi-verse catalogues of 25:35-38 and reduces them to a formula.
verses.40:
> They have certainly passed by the city ˹of Sodom˺, which had been showered with a dreadful rain ˹of stones˺. Have they not seen its ruins? But they do not expect to be resurrected

**The City the Disbelievers Walked Past**

The verse addresses the disbelievers of Makkah directly, connecting the catalogue of destroyed peoples to their own experience: *wa la-qad ātaw ʿalā'l-qaryati'llatī umṭirat matra'r-saw'* — "And they have certainly passed by the city that was showered with a dreadful rain." The city is Sodom, the community of the prophet Lot, which was destroyed by a rain of stones (7:84; 11:82; 15:73-74; 26:173; 27:58; 29:34; 51:33-34). The Quraysh, in their trade journeys to Syria and the north, would have passed through or near the region where Lot's people lived, and the ruins would have been visible. The word *ātaw* (they have passed by) is in the past tense — they have already done this, they have already seen the ruins — and the question that follows — *a-falam yakūnū yarawnahā* — "Have they not seen it?" — assumes the answer is yes.

The rhetorical force is enormous. The disbelievers demand signs (25:7-8, 25:21), and the sūrah points out that they have already walked through the most vivid sign available: the ruins of a community that was destroyed for the same kind of rejection they are now committing. The ruins are not hidden; they are on the road. The evidence is not abstract; it is physical. The disbelievers do not need an angel to descend or a treasure to appear; they need only to look at what they have already seen and draw the conclusion. The verse's question — "Have they not seen it?" — is the sūrah's most direct challenge: the sign is already in front of you, and you have walked past it without understanding.

**Matra'r-Saw': The Rain of Stones**

Al-Ṭabarī connects the word *saw'* (evil, dreadful) with the nature of the rain: it was not ordinary rain that nourishes but rain that destroys, rain that falls with the force and the intent of a weapon. The same word appears in 27:58 — "And We rained upon them a rain, and evil was the rain of those who were warned" — where the adjective *saw'* is applied directly to the rain itself. The rain is "evil" not because of a moral quality but because of its effect: it killed, it destroyed, it erased.

**The Ruins as Evidence for the Resurrection**

The verse's final clause — "But they do not expect to be resurrected" — connects the ruins of Sodom to the sūrah's central theological claim: the denial of the Hour (25:11) is the root of every other error. The disbelievers pass by the ruins, see the physical evidence of divine punishment, and draw no conclusion because they do not expect the resurrection. The word *yarjūna* (expect, hope, anticipate) appears in 25:21 in the same context — "those who do not expect to meet Us" — and the repetition links 25:40 back to the diagnosis in 25:11. Each return adds a new layer of evidence: the first return (25:11) names the denial; the second (25:21) shows its consequences; the third (25:40) grounds it in physical reality. The ruins of Sodom are the final evidence, and the question — "Have they not seen it?" — is the final challenge.
verses.41:
> When they see you ˹O Prophet˺, they only make fun of you, ˹saying,˺ “Is this the one that Allah has sent as a messenger

**Mockery as a Response to the Unfamiliar**

The verse describes a specific social behavior: the disbelievers see the Prophet ﷺ and immediately begin to ridicule him. The word *yahzarūnaka* (they mock you, they make fun of you) names the act precisely — it is not argument, not debate, not engagement with the message, but derision directed at the person. The mockers do not ask "Is this message true?" They ask "Is this the one God sent?" The question targets the messenger, not the message, and it assumes the answer is no. The grammar of the question — *a-hādhā'lladhī ba'atha'llāhu rasūlā* — is a rhetorical construction that expects rejection: the very phrasing implies that the person in front of them cannot possibly be the answer to the question of who God would send.

This pattern of mockery is not unique to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The Qur'an records the same response from every prophetic community: "How many a prophet did We send to those of old! Yet never did a prophet come to them but they mocked him" (43:6-7). The mockery of Noah (26:116), Hud (26:141), Salih (26:141), Lot (26:165), and Shu'ayb (26:176) follows the same script — a righteous person arrives, and the community's first response is not reflection but ridicule. The recurrence of the pattern across prophetic history tells the reader something about the nature of the human response to divine guidance: the first instinct is not to examine but to dismiss, and the dismissal takes the form of mockery because mockery is the cheapest form of rejection. It costs nothing, requires no evidence, and produces immediate social solidarity among the mockers.

**The Mockery of the Prophet's Followers**

Al-Qurṭubī connects this verse with the broader Qur'anic theme of the disbelievers' incredulity at God's choice of followers. In 11:27, the disbelievers say of Noah's followers, "We see that none follow you but the lowliest among us." In 46:11, the disbelievers say of the Muslims, "Had this Quran been anything good, they would not have preceded us to it." The pattern is consistent: the disbelievers judge the message by the social status of its followers. Because the early Muslims were predominantly poor and socially marginal, the message is dismissed as unworthy. The mockery in 25:41 targets the Prophet directly, but the same mockery extends to everyone who follows him. The social logic is circular: the message is rejected because its followers are lowly, and the followers are lowly because the message is rejected. The Qur'an breaks the circle by insisting that God's criteria for worthiness are not the same as the Quraysh's criteria, and that the lowly in this world may be the exalted in the next.

**The Verse’s Role in the Sūrah’s Structure**

Verse 25:41 opens the second cycle of disbelievers’ objections in the sūrah. The first cycle (25:4-8) focused on the Quran and the Prophet’s credentials; the second cycle (25:41-44) focuses on the social dynamics of rejection. The shift is from theology to sociology: the disbelievers’ objections are no longer about the message’s content but about the messenger’s social acceptability. The mockery in 25:41 is a social act, performed in public, designed to enforce the boundary between the followers and the non-followers. The sūrah’s placement of this social dynamic after the catalogue of natural signs (25:45-50) and before the Last-Day warnings (25:11-19) serves a specific purpose: it shows that the disbelievers’ rejection is not based on evidence but on social pressure. The signs are there; the evidence is clear; and the disbelievers reject it not because it is insufficient but because accepting it would cost them their social standing. The mockery is the price they charge for acceptance, and the price is the evidence of their priorities.
verses.42:
> He would have almost tricked us away from our gods, had we not been so devoted to them.” ˹But˺ soon they will know, when they face the punishment, who is far astray from the ˹Right˺ Way

**The Punishment as the Judge**

The second half of the verse — *sa-yaʿlamūna ʿinda ra'yati'l-ʿadhābi man aḍallu sabīlā* — shifts to the future: "They will know, when they face the punishment, who is farther astray from the Way." The punishment itself will serve as the judge. The disbelievers believed they were on the right path; the believers believed the disbelievers were on the wrong path. The disagreement cannot be resolved in this life because both sides claim the same thing: that the other is astray. The verse resolves the disagreement by pointing to the punishment as the final arbiter. When the punishment arrives, it will settle the question not by argument but by demonstration. The one who is astray will be the one who suffers, and the suffering will be the proof.

The word *sabīl* (Way, path) recurs in this verse for the eleventh time in the sūrah, maintaining the thread that runs from 25:9 (the disbelievers who "could not find the Way") through 25:27 (the wrongdoer who wishes he "had taken a Way with the Messenger") to 25:34 (those who are "farthest from the Right Way"). The repetition of *sabīl* across the sūrah creates a continuous argument: the Way was offered, the Way was refused, and the punishment will reveal who was on the Way and who was not. The disbelievers in 25:42 claim steadfastness; the punishment will show that their steadfastness was the very thing that kept them from the Way.

**The Imminence of the Warning**

The word *sa-ʿarafūna* or *sa-yaʿlamūna* ("they will soon know") uses the prefix *sa-*, which in Arabic indicates the near future — something that will happen soon, imminently, without delay. The Qur'an does not say "they will eventually know" or "they will one day know"; it says they will soon know. The imminence is part of the warning: the punishment is not distant, not theoretical, not reserved for a far-off Day. It is approaching, and the approach is measured in the present tense. This urgency appears across the Qur'an's warning passages: "The Hour has drawn near" (54:1); "The reckoning of the people has drawn near, yet they are in heedlessness, turning away" (21:1). The disbelievers of Makkah live in the interval between the warning and its fulfillment, and the interval is shorter than they think.

**The Disbelievers’ Use of Sabr**

The disbelievers’ claim that they were “steadfast” upon their gods is one of the sūrah’s sharpest ironies. The word sabr (patience, steadfastness) is the quality the Qur’an most consistently demands of the believers. In 25:20 the Prophet is asked, “Will you not then be patient?” (25:20) In 31:17 the command is, “Be patient. The promise of Allah is true.” In 46:35 the instruction is, “So be patient, as the messengers of strong resolve were patient.” The disbelievers in 25:42 use the same word for their attachment to idols. The misuse of sabr reveals the moral neutrality of the virtue itself: patience is valuable only when it is applied to the right object. Patient attachment to falsehood is not a virtue but a vice, and the disbelievers’ steadfastness in the service of idols is the mirror image of the believers’ steadfastness in the service of God.
verses.43:
> Have you seen ˹O Prophet˺ the one who has taken their own desires as their god? Will you then be a keeper over them

**Desire as a False God**

The verse poses a rhetorical question that redefines idolatry: *a-ra'ayta mani ittakhadhha ilāhahu hawāhu* — "Have you considered the one who has made desire his god?" The word *hawā* (desire, passion, caprice) refers to the inclinations of the lower self — the pull toward comfort, pleasure, status. Self-gratification that competes with the pull of divine guidance. By calling *hawā* a god (*ilāh*), the verse performs a theological reclassification. The disbelievers who worship idols are, in this verse, revealed to be worshipping something deeper than wood and stone: they are worshipping themselves — specifically, the part of themselves that resists submission to anything greater than its own appetites.

The redefinition is not metaphorical. The Qur'an elsewhere makes the same move: "Have you seen the one who takes his desire as his god, and God leads him astray knowingly" (45:23). In that verse, the connection between desire-as-god and divine misguidance is explicit: the person who worships desire is allowed by God to follow it to its logical end, and the end is misguidance. The connection in 25:43 is subtler but identical in structure. The disbelievers' attachment to their idols is not a reasoned theological commitment; it is an expression of desire — the desire to maintain their social order, their habits, their comfort, their identity. The idols are the visible form of the desire; the desire is the real object of worship.

**The Prophet's Role: Messenger, Not Warden**

The same rebuke appears in 88:21-22: "So remind, for you are only a reminder; you are not a warder over them." The Prophet's role is defined by its limits: he delivers the message, and God handles the consequences. The disbelievers who have taken desire as their god are beyond the Prophet's reach — not because the message is insufficient, but because their attachment to desire has closed the door that the message was designed to open. The verse's question — "Will you then be a keeper over them?" — is God's way of telling the Prophet to let go: the responsibility for their guidance was never his, and the responsibility for their misguidance is not his either.

**The Prophetic Rejection of Wardenship**

The command to the Prophet in the second half of 25:43 — “Will you then be a keeper over them?” (25:43) — defines the limits of prophetic responsibility. The Prophet’s role is to deliver the message, not to enforce compliance. The distinction is crucial because it removes the burden of the disbelievers’ rejection from the Prophet’s shoulders. He has delivered the message; the message has been heard; and the disbelievers have chosen to follow their desires instead. The choice is theirs, and the consequence is theirs. The question “Will you then be a keeper over them?” (25:43) is God’s way of releasing the Prophet from a responsibility that was never his.

The same principle appears in 88:21-22: “So remind, for you are only a reminder; you are not a warder over them.” (88:22) (88:22) The Prophet’s grief over his people’s rejection (25:30) was real, but the grief does not create a responsibility to force them to accept what they refuse.
verses.44:
> Or do you think that most of them listen or understand? They are only like cattle—no, more than that, they are astray from the ˹Right˺ Way

**The Refusal to Listen and the Refusal to Understand**

The verse addresses the Prophet with another rhetorical question: *am taḥsabu anna aktharahum yasma'ūna aw ya'qilūna* — "Or do you think that most of them listen or understand?" The question expects a negative answer: no, they do not listen, and no, they do not understand. The two verbs — *yasma'ūna* (to hear, to listen) and *ya'qilūna* (to reason, to understand) — cover the two stages of comprehension. First, the sound must enter the ear; then, the mind must process it into meaning. The disbelievers fail at both. They do not hear the Quran's message — not because their ears are blocked but because their attention is elsewhere, fixed on desire (25:43), on social standing (25:41), on the preservation of their inherited customs (25:42). And even when the words do reach them, they do not reason their way to understanding — not because their minds are deficient but because understanding would require them to act on what they understand, and action would require them to change.

**The Cattle Comparison and Its Limitations**

The comparison — *innahum illā ka'l-an'ām* — "They are only like cattle" — is one of the Qur'an's harshest judgments. The same comparison appears in 7:179 — "They are like cattle; rather, they are more astray" — and in 25:44 the same intensifier appears: *bal hum aḍallu sabīlā* — "rather, they are more astray from the Way." The comparison is not to insult but to diagnose. Cattle follow their instincts — they eat, drink, sleep, and reproduce, driven by appetite and habit. The disbelievers do the same: they eat, drink, accumulate wealth, and reproduce, driven by desire and custom. The parallel is precise: both operate at the level of appetite, without submitting their appetites to a higher purpose.

**The Word Sabīl and the Sūrah's Persistent Thread**

The phrase *aḍallu sabīlā* — "more astray from the Way" — repeats the sūrah's central motif for the twelfth time. The word *sabīl* (Way, path) has appeared in 25:9, 25:10, 25:27, 25:34, 25:42, and now 25:44, each time in the context of guidance either offered or refused. The repetition is not decorative; it is the sūrah's way of insisting that there is a Way, that the Way is available, and that the disbelievers' condition is not a matter of fate but of choice. Cattle do not have a Way; they have instinct. Human beings have a Way — the Criterion (25:1), the Messenger (25:56), the Reminder (25:29) — and the refusal to walk it is the defining error the sūrah describes. The comparison to cattle is therefore not a final judgment but an intermediate one: the disbelievers are behaving like animals, but they are not animals, and the Day of Judgment will hold them to the standard of the faculties they refused to use.
verses.45:
> Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shade—He could have simply made it ˹remain˺ still if He so willed—then We make the sun its guide

**The Shade as a Sign of Divine Sovereignty**

The verse begins a new section of the sūrah — a sustained meditation on natural phenomena as evidence of God's power and wisdom. The first sign is the shade (*ẓill*): *a-lam tara ilā Rabbika kayfa madda'ẓ-ẓill* — "Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shade?" The verb *madda* (to extend, to stretch out) describes the gradual movement of shadow across the earth as the sun moves through the sky. The shade is not static; it lengthens, shortens, and shifts direction throughout the day, responding to the sun's position. The verse invites the Prophet — and through him, the reader — to observe this daily phenomenon and recognize the divine hand behind it.

**The Spiritual Allegory of Shade and Light**

Several commentators, including Ibn ʿAjībah, read verses 25:45-46 as a spiritual allegory. The shade represents the human soul — or every created thing — which is a shadow cast from the Unseen. The sun represents sacred knowledge, which illuminates the soul's true nature and causes the shadow of ignorance to retreat. The gradual withdrawal of the shade (25:46) represents the process of spiritual purification, in which the soul is drawn gradually toward God until it is annihilated (*fanā'*) in the divine light. The allegory is not the verse's primary meaning — the primary meaning is a sign in the natural world — but it shows the Qur'an's capacity to operate on multiple levels simultaneously. The physical phenomenon (shade moving in response to the sun) points to a spiritual truth (the soul moving in response to divine knowledge), and both point to the same conclusion: everything in creation is guided by a power beyond itself.

**The Shade as a Metaphor for the Temporary**

The shade in 25:45 is, at one level, a physical phenomenon — the shadow cast by the earth as the sun moves across the sky. But the shade also carries a metaphorical weight that the Qur’an develops elsewhere. In 13:15 — “Whatever is in the heavens and earth prostrates to Allah, willingly or unwillingly, and their shadows in the morning and afternoon” — the shadows themselves are described as worshipping God. In 25:45-46, the shade is extended, guided by the sun, and then withdrawn toward God. The sequence — extension, guidance, withdrawal — mirrors the arc of every created thing: it comes into existence, it is guided through its term, and it returns to its source. The shade is temporary by nature; it exists only in relation to the light that casts it, and when the light changes, the shade changes with it. The human being is, in this reading, a shade — a temporary existence cast by a permanent light, destined to be withdrawn when the light shifts. The metaphor is not the verse’s primary meaning, but it enriches the observation and shows the Qur’an’s capacity to operate on multiple registers simultaneously.
verses.46:
> causing the shade to retreat gradually

**The Gentle Withdrawal**

The verse is compressed to a single clause: *thumma qabadnāhu ilaynā qabḍan yasīrā* — "then We withdraw it to Ourselves, a gentle withdrawal." The word *qabadnā* (We seize, We withdraw) describes the act of pulling the shade back. The pronoun *ilaynā* (to Us, toward Ourselves) names the direction: the shade is drawn toward God. The image is of a curtain being pulled back by an unseen hand — not torn away, not suddenly removed, but drawn gently, gradually, until what was hidden behind the shade is fully revealed. The word *yasīr* (gentle, easy, light) describes the quality of the withdrawal: it is not violent, not abrupt, not painful. The shade retreats step by step, and each step is barely noticeable. The transition from darkness to light, from shadow to illumination, happens so smoothly that the eye does not register the change until it is complete.

Al-Ṭabarī glosses *yasīr* as "quickly" or "in a hidden way," while al-Zamakhsharī reads it as "gradually." The two readings are not contradictory: the withdrawal is both gentle and imperceptible — it happens quickly enough that it seems sudden only in retrospect. Gradually enough that it does not disturb the creatures who depend on the shade. The dual quality — speed and gentleness — mirrors the Qur'an's description of divine action elsewhere: "His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it 'Be!' and it is" (36:82).

**The Connotation of the Hour**

Al-Rāzī observes that the word *yasīr* (easy, gentle) carries a secondary connotation related to the Hour — the end of the world. In 29:19 — "Do they not see how Allah originates creation and then reproduces it? That is easy for Allah" — the word *yasīr* describes God's power to create and re-create. In 50:44 — "The Day the earth breaks away from them, and they emerge; that is an easy gathering for Us" — the same word describes the ease of the resurrection. The withdrawal of the shade in 25:46, read alongside these passages, becomes a parable of the Hour: just as the shade is gently withdrawn toward God, so the created order will be gently withdrawn toward its Maker. The ease of the withdrawal is the point: what seems impossible to human beings — the end of the world, the resurrection of the dead — is, for God, as easy as the movement of a shadow across the ground. The word yasīr (gentle, easy) in 25:46 describes the quality of God’s withdrawal of the shade, and the same word appears in other Qur’anic passages to describe the ease of divine action. The ease is not a diminishment of the act but a revelation of the actor: the power that withdraws the shade is the same power that will withdraw the world, and both withdrawals are gentle, gradual, and certain.
verses.47:
> He is the One Who has made the night for you as a cover, and ˹made˺ sleep for resting, and the day for rising

**Night as a Garment**

The verse describes three gifts of God in a single sentence: night, sleep, and day. The night is called *libās* — a garment, a covering, something that wraps around the body and conceals it. The metaphor is precise: just as a garment protects the body from cold and exposure, the night protects human beings from the exhaustion of constant activity. The darkness is not a deficiency but a mercy — it provides the conditions under which rest becomes possible. Without night, there would be no pause, no interval of stillness, no period in which the body and mind can recover from the demands of the day. The word *libās* (garment) implies intimacy: the night does not merely exist around the human being; it wraps around them, covering them as a garment covers the body.

The same metaphor appears in 78:10 — "And We made the night as a covering" — where the sense of envelopment is the same. The night is one of God's most basic gifts, so basic that it is easily overlooked. The sūrah's placement of this observation in the midst of its arguments against the disbelievers serves a specific purpose: the same God who threatens the disbelievers with punishment also provides them with the nightly rest that sustains their lives. The mercy and the warning come from the same source, and the disbelievers' failure to recognize the source in either case is the error the sūrah diagnoses.

**Sleep as Death's Brother**

The word *subātan* (sleep, rest) is described as something God "made" — *ja'ala* — placing it in the same category as night and day: not a natural occurrence but a divine provision. Al-Ṭabarī notes the Arabic proverb "Sleep is the brother of death" (*al-nawm akhu'l-mawt*), and the Qur'an itself draws the connection: "God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died, during their sleep" (39:42). Sleep, in this reading, is a minor death — a temporary removal of the soul from the body, a rehearsal for the permanent removal that death will bring. The body lies still, the senses are suspended, and the person exists in a state that is, experientially, indistinguishable from death. The difference is that sleep is reversible and death is not — but the experience is the same, and the sameness is the lesson. The disbelievers who deny the resurrection (25:11) undergo a miniature version of it every night and do not recognize it.

**The Verse's Connection to the Sūrah's Warnings**

The description of night, sleep, and day in 25:47 is not a digression from the sūrah's argument but a continuation of it. The sūrah has described the punishment of the disbelievers in the fire (25:11-14), the reward of the righteous in the garden (25:15-16), and the natural signs that point to God's power (25:45-46). The connection between the daily sign and the Last-Day reality is the sūrah's way of saying: the resurrection is not an extraordinary claim; it is the natural extension of an ordinary experience. The disbelievers who accept the daily cycle without recognizing its theological implications are living inside the evidence and refusing to read it.
verses.48:
> And He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy, and We send down pure rain from the sky

**Winds as Harbingers of Mercy**

The verse continues the catalogue of natural signs that began in 25:45. The winds are described as *mubashshirāt* — bearers of good news, heralds of glad tidings — sent ahead of God's mercy (*raḥmah*). The mercy in question is rain, and the winds are its advance guard. In the Arabian climate, the arrival of wind signaled the approach of rain clouds — a sequence so regular that it became a sign the audience could recognize without being told. The word *mubashshirāt* (bearers of good news) is the same word used for the angels who bring good news to the righteous at death (16:32; 41:30). The parallel is deliberate: the winds that herald rain are doing the same work as the angels who herald reward — they are messengers of mercy, announcing what is about to arrive.

The connection between wind and rain appears throughout the Qur'an. In 7:57 — "It is He who sends the winds as good news before His mercy, until when they carry heavy rain clouds, We drive them to a dead land and send down rain, bringing forth all kinds of fruits" — the same sequence is described in greater detail: the winds carry the clouds, the clouds release the rain, and the rain brings dead land to life. In 30:46 — "Among His signs is that He sends the winds bearing good news, so that He may make you taste His mercy" — the tasting of mercy through rain is made explicit. The sūrah's use of this image in 25:48 adds to its catalogue of signs: after the shade (25:45-46) and the night, sleep, and day (25:47), the winds and rain complete the picture of a world designed for human benefit.

**Pure Rain: The Word *Mubārak**

The word *ṭahūr* also connects to the Qur'anic concept of ritual purification. In 8:11 — "He sent down upon you water from the sky to purify you by this" — rain is described as a means of spiritual as well as physical cleansing. The rain that washes the earth also washes the soul, and the regularity of the rain — season after season, year after year — is a regular renewal of the opportunity for purification.
