The disbelievers who receive the rain and do not recognize its source are receiving mercy they do not acknowledge, and the unacknowledged mercy becomes, on the Day of Judgment, an additional count in the case against them.

**Rain as the Sustaining Gift**

The rain described in 25:48 is not only water falling from the sky; it is a comprehensive provision that sustains every form of life on earth. The rain feeds the rivers, waters the crops, nourishes the livestock, fills the wells, and replenishes the aquifers that supply human communities. The word ṭahūr (pure, purifying) applied to the rain describes both its physical quality — clean, drinkable, life-giving — and its spiritual quality — a reminder of God’s mercy that purifies the soul of ingratitude. The Qur’an’s consistent pairing of rain with divine mercy (7:57; 16:10; 25:48; 30:24) establishes a theological framework in which the natural world is not a neutral backdrop but a continuous expression of God’s care.

The catalogue of natural signs in 25:45-48 — shade, night, sleep, day, wind, rain — serves as the sūrah's alternative to the spectacular signs the disbelievers demanded.
verses.49:
> giving life to a lifeless land, and providing water for countless animals and humans of Our Own creation

**The Resurrection of Dead Land**

The verse continues the description of rain's purpose: *li-nuḥyiya bihi balḍatan maytan* — "so that We may give life by this to a dead land." The word *mayt* (dead) applied to land describes earth that has been stripped of vegetation, color, and vitality — desert, parched ground, land that produces nothing. The rain transforms this dead land into something living: seeds germinate, grasses grow, the brown expanse turns green. The transformation is one of the most visible and dramatic signs in the natural world, and the Qur'an uses it repeatedly as an analogy for the resurrection of the dead. In 22:5 — "You see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every delightful pair" — the same observation is made with the same implication: the God who brings dead land to life can bring dead bodies to life. In 30:50 — "Look at the effects of God's mercy: how He gives life to the earth after its death. Verily, that is the One who will give life to the dead, and He has power over all things" — the connection is made explicit.

**The Continuity of the Sign Catalogue**

Verse 25:49 continues the natural sign catalogue that began in 25:45. The sequence — shade (45-46), night-sleep-day (47), wind and rain (48), revival of dead land (49) — builds a cumulative argument. Each sign adds a new dimension of divine power: the ability to move shadows, to create the cycle of rest and waking, to send winds that herald rain, and to bring dead earth to life. The cumulative effect is stronger than any single sign because it shows not one act of power but a sustained pattern of provision. The sūrah is not asking the disbelievers to believe based on a single miracle; it is asking them to observe the world they already live in and recognize the power behind it. The world is full of signs, and the signs all point in the same direction. The disbelievers' refusal to follow the signs is not a failure of evidence but a failure of will, and the sūrah names the failure in the verse that follows (25:50).

**The Verse’s Contribution to the Sūrah’s Argument**

Verse 25:49 adds the most dramatic of the natural signs to the catalogue: the revival of dead land by rain. The drama lies in the visibility of the transformation — a barren desert becomes, within days of rainfall, a carpet of green. The transformation is not hidden or rare; it is one of the most visible and recurring phenomena in the natural world, and the Qur’an uses it as the primary analogy for the resurrection of the dead. The sūrah’s placement of this sign after the description of rain (25:48) and before the statement about human ingratitude (25:50) creates a specific argumentative sequence: God sends the rain, God revives the land, and the people who receive both are ungrateful. The sequence mirrors the sūrah’s larger argument: God sends the revelation, God guides the community, and the disbelievers who receive both are ungrateful. The parallel between rain and revelation, between the revival of land and the revival of hearts, is the sūrah’s way of saying that the Quran is as necessary, as available. As life-giving as rain, and the rejection of the Quran is as irrational as the refusal to drink the water that sustains life.
verses.50:
> We certainly disperse it among them so they may be mindful, but most people persist in ungratefulness

**Most People Persist in Ingratitude**

The verse's second clause — *wa aktharu'n-nāsi illā kafarū* — states the outcome of the test: "but most people persist in ungratefulness." The word *kafarū* (they disbelieved, they were ungrateful, they covered over) carries the dual meaning that the Qur'an consistently assigns to *kufr*: denial of God and ingratitude for His gifts. The rain falls, the land produces, the animals are fed, and the people who receive all of this attribute it to something other than God — to the stars, to the weather, to their own ingenuity, to chance. The attribution is an act of *kufr* because it covers over (*k-f-r* literally means "to cover") the truth of the source. The rain is the evidence; the source is God; and the refusal to acknowledge the source is the covering-over that the word *kufr* names.

Al-Iṣfahānī and al-Qurṭubī note that the practice of attributing rainfall to the rising and setting of certain stars was common among the pre-Islamic Arabs. The Qur'an addresses this directly in 52:49 — "And in the alternation of night and day. In what God sends down from the sky of provision by which He gives life to the earth after its death. In the directing of the winds — truly there are signs for people who use reason" — where the natural phenomena the Arabs attributed to stars are explicitly attributed to God. Verse 25:50 names the attribution to stars as a form of *kufr* — not atheism in the modern sense but a misattribution that denies God's direct involvement in the provision of sustenance.

**The Relationship Between Rain and Revelation**

The placement of the rain sign immediately after the disbelievers' mockery (25:41-44) and before the command to strive with the Quran (25:52) creates a structural parallel between rain and revelation. Both are sent down from above; both are distributed according to God's wisdom; both are designed to produce *tadhakkur* (mindfulness); and both are rejected by most people. The rain falls on disbelievers and believers alike, and the Quran is recited for disbelievers and believers alike. The disbelievers receive both and respond with *kufr* — covering over the truth of the source. The parallel between rain and revelation is the sūrah's way of saying that the Quran is as natural, as necessary, and as available as rain, and the rejection of the Quran is as irrational as the refusal to acknowledge the source of the water that sustains life.

**The Verse’s Role in the Sūrah’s Argument**

Verse 25:50 closes the natural sign catalogue that began in 25:45 and transitions to the next section of the sūrah. The transition is from observation to command: after demonstrating God’s power through the signs of shade, night, sleep, day, wind, rain, and the revival of dead land, the sūrah will command the Prophet to strive with the Quran (25:52). The statement that “most people persist in ungratefulness” is the bridge between the two sections: the signs have been presented, the evidence has been offered, and the result is that most people remain unconvinced. The failure of the evidence to produce universal faith is not a failure of the evidence but a failure of the audience, and the failure is the reason the striving is necessary. If the signs were enough on their own, no striving would be needed. Because most people resist the signs, the Prophet must strive with the Quran — the instrument that interprets the signs and gives them their meaning. The sūrah’s structure thus moves from the sign to the interpreter, from the evidence to the voice that explains it.
verses.51:
> Had We willed, We could have easily sent a warner to every society

The verse presents a counterfactual: *wa law shi'nā la-baʿthnā fī kulli qaryatin nadhīrān* — "Had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town." The counterfactual serves a specific purpose: it magnifies the status of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ by showing what God did not do. God could have sent a warner to every town — a separate prophet for each community, as in earlier times — but He chose instead to send one Prophet to all of humanity. The singling out is not a limitation but a honor: the Prophet who carries the final message must be extraordinary enough to carry it alone, and the message must be universal enough to reach every town without being re-sent.

**The Contrast Between Rain and Revelation**

The verse follows the description of rain falling on many lands (25:48-50), and the contrast is deliberate. Rain is distributed universally — it falls on every town, every land, every community. Revelation, in the final dispensation, is sent through one person to all communities. The rain reaches everyone directly; the revelation reaches everyone through a single channel. The comparison highlights the different modes of divine provision: physical sustenance (rain) is given directly to all; spiritual guidance (revelation) is given through a messenger to all. The disbelievers who acknowledged the rain as a natural phenomenon but rejected the revelation as a human invention were accepting one form of divine provision while refusing the other. The verse names the refusal and shows that it was not inevitable — God could have sent a warner to every town, but He chose to send one to all of them, and the choice was an act of trust in the Prophet's capacity and the message's universality.

**The Verse’s Theological Implication**

The verse’s counterfactual — “Had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town” — implies that God’s choice of a single messenger was deliberate, not arbitrary. The singling out of the Prophet Muhammad for the final, universal message was a decision made in divine wisdom, and the decision reflects God’s knowledge of the Prophet’s capacity and the message’s sufficiency. The verse does not explain why God chose one messenger instead of many; it simply states the choice and, in stating it, honors the chosen. The Prophet’s burden is heavier than any earlier prophet’s, but the honor is proportionate: the one who carries the final message to all of humanity has been judged capable of carrying it alone. The sūrah’s placement of this verse after the statement about human ingratitude (25:50) and before the command to strive (25:52) creates a specific message: the Prophet’s task is difficult, the audience is resistant, and the response is not despair but effort. The “great striving” of 25:52 is the human response to the divine choice of 25:51. This cooperative dynamic — God chooses, and the chosen one strives — is the fundamental pattern of prophetic mission throughout the Qur’an.
verses.52:
> So do not yield to the disbelievers, but strive diligently against them with this ˹Quran˺

The verse issues a direct command to the Prophet: *falā tuṭiʿi'l-kāfirīna wa jāhidhum bihi jihādan kabīrān* — "So do not obey the disbelievers. Strive against them with it — a great striving." The word *lā tuṭiʿ* (do not obey) is addressed to the Prophet in the singular, making it personal: this is not a general instruction to the community but a specific instruction to the messenger.

The *jihād* in this verse is not military — al-Qurṭubī and others explicitly state that this is a Makkan sūrah and the permission to fight had not yet been given. The instrument of the striving is specified: *bihi* — "with it," referring to the Quran itself.

**The Word "With It": The Quran as the Instrument**

The pronoun *bihi* ("with it") in the phrase "strive against them with it" identifies the Quran as the instrument of *jihād*. This is one of the most significant statements in the sūrah about the nature of the prophetic mission: the Prophet's primary tool is not political power, military force, or social leverage — it is the text itself. The Quran is the Criterion (25:1), the Reminder (25:29), the message that distinguishes truth from falsehood (25:1), and it is also the weapon with which the Prophet is commanded to strive. The striving is not physical combat but textual engagement: presenting the Quran's arguments, answering the disbelievers' objections (25:33), and maintaining the message's clarity against every try to distort or dismiss it.

Al-Ṭabarī notes that the phrase "with it" makes the Quran both the message and the means of delivering the message. The Prophet does not need another tool; the Quran is enough for every argument the disbelievers raise, and the sūrah has showed this by recording the disbelievers' objections (25:4-8, 25:21) and God's responses (25:6, 25:10-16, 25:20, 25:33). The pattern is the instruction: the Prophet's role is to deliver the Quran's answers to the disbelievers' questions, and the delivery itself is the striving. The command in 25:52 is therefore not a call to violence but a call to persistence — to continue delivering the message regardless of the opposition, and to use the message itself as the instrument of opposition.

**The Verse’s Role in the Sūrah’s Structure**

Verse 25:52 is the pivot between the sūrah’s catalogue of natural signs (25:45-50) and its catalogue of divine signs in the physical world (25:53-55). After demonstrating God’s power through shade, night, day, wind, rain, and the revival of dead land, the sūrah commands the Prophet to use the Quran as the instrument of striving. The command marks a transition from observation to action: the signs have been seen, the evidence has been presented, and now the Prophet must act on what the evidence shows. The instrument of action is specified: the Quran. The Prophet does not need another tool; the Quran is the Criterion (25:1), the Reminder (25:29), and the instrument of striving (25:52). The sūrah’s structure thus moves from the natural world to the revealed text, from the sign to the interpreter, and from the observation to the command. The movement is the sūrah’s way of saying: the signs are evidence, and the Quran is the voice that gives the evidence its meaning.
verses.53:
> And He is the One Who merges the two bodies of water: one fresh and palatable and the other salty and bitter, placing between them a barrier they cannot cross

**The Two Seas and Their Separation**

The verse describes another sign in the natural world: the meeting of two bodies of water — one fresh and sweet (*'adhb furāt*), the other salty and bitter (*milḥ ujāj*) — and the barrier (*barzakh*) that prevents them from merging. The phenomenon is observable at estuaries and river mouths around the world, where freshwater rivers flow into the salty ocean and the two waters remain distinct for a measurable distance before gradually mixing. The Qur'an's observation of this phenomenon is not only scientific but theological: the separation is a sign of divine power, because the natural tendency of two liquids placed in contact is to mix, and the maintenance of the boundary requires a force that opposes the tendency.

The word *barzakh* (barrier, isthmus, partition) appears in the Qur'an in both physical and Last-Day contexts. In 23:100 — "And behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected" — the *barzakh* refers to the interval between death and resurrection, the state in which the dead exist before the Day of Judgment. In 55:19-20 — "He released the two seas, meeting side by side; between them is a barrier which they do not transgress" — the same physical phenomenon is described with the same word. The dual usage — physical barrier and Last-Day interval — suggests that the *barzakh* is a principle, not merely a phenomenon: God places barriers between things that should not mix, and the barriers hold because God wills them to hold. The fresh water and the salt water are kept apart by the same power that keeps the living and the dead apart.

**The Repeated Structure of the Sign Catalogue**

Verse 25:53 continues the pattern established in 25:45: each verse presents a natural phenomenon and identifies it as a sign of God's power. The shade (45-46), the night-sleep-day cycle (47), the winds and rain (48-49), and now the two seas (53) form a chain of evidence, each link adding a new dimension to the argument. The chain will continue with human creation (25:54), and the cumulative effect is a worldview in which every observable phenomenon — from the movement of shadows to the mixing of waters — is evidence of the One who controls it. The sūrah does not ask the disbelievers to believe based on a single sign; it asks them to observe the totality of the created world and recognize the power behind it. The totality is the argument, and the argument is addressed to people who have eyes and refuse to see.

**The Verse’s Connection to the Sūrah’s Earlier Uses of Barzakh**

The word barzakh (barrier) appears earlier in the sūrah in a very different context: in 25:22, the disbelievers cry “Ḥijran maḥjūrā!” (“A barrier, forbidden!”) when they see the angels on the Day of Judgment. The echo between 25:22 and 25:53 is deliberate: the same word that names the barrier between fresh and salt water names the barrier the disbelievers will erect between themselves and the angels. In both cases, the barrier is something God maintains: the physical barrier keeps the waters from mixing; the Last-Day barrier keeps the disbelievers from receiving mercy. The repetition of barzakh across the sūrah creates a thematic link between the natural world and the Hereafter, between the signs in creation and the consequences in judgment. The barrier that the disbelievers cry out for on the Day of Judgment is the same kind of barrier that God places between the mixable and the unmixable in the natural world — a boundary that holds because God wills it to hold.
verses.54:
> And He is the One Who creates human beings from a ˹humble˺ liquid, then establishes for them bonds of kinship and marriage. For your Lord is Most Capable

**The Theology of Human Origin**

The verse's mention of human creation from water connects to other Qur'anic passages that describe the same process. In 21:30 — "We made from water every living thing" — the principle is universal: all life depends on water. In 24:45 — "Allah has created every animal from water" — the same universality is stated. In 32:7-8 — "He began the creation of man from clay, then made his progeny from an extract of despised water" — the specific application to human beings is made. The Qur'an's consistent use of water as the origin of life serves a theological purpose: it establishes the humility of human origins and, by contrast, the grandeur of God's creative power. The same God who created the heavens and the earth (25:59) also created human beings from water, and the disparity between the origin and the outcome is the measure of His power.

**The Connection to the Disbelievers' Rejection**

The verse's placement in the sūrah after the command to strive with the Quran (25:52) and the sign of the two seas (25:53) creates a specific argumentative context. The disbelievers who deny God's power are reminded that they themselves are evidence of it. They were created from water, their families were established by God, and their marriages were designed by God. The social world they inhabit — the tribal structures, the family alliances, the kinship networks — is a product of divine design, not human effort. The disbelievers who attribute their social order to their own ingenuity or to the traditions of their forefathers are ignoring the most basic fact about their existence: they began as a drop of fluid. Everything they are was made from that drop by a power they did not choose and cannot control. The verse ends with *wa Rabbuka Qadīr* — "and your Lord is Most Capable" — a declaration that closes the argument: the God who created you from nothing is capable of doing whatever He wills, including the resurrection you deny.

**The Verse’s Placement in the Sūrah’s Argument**

Verse 25:54 continues the catalogue of divine signs in creation that began with the shade (25:45) and continued through the night-sleep-day cycle (25:47), the winds and rain (25:48-49), the two seas (25:53), and now the creation of human beings and the establishment of kinship and marriage. The sequence builds a comprehensive picture of divine providence: God controls the atmosphere (shade, wind, rain), the hydrosphere (the two seas), and the biosphere (human creation and social organization). The sūrah’s catalogue is not random but systematic: it moves from the outer world to the inner world, from the signs that surround the human being to the signs that constitute the human being. The creation from water, the establishment of kinship, and the design of marriage are the most intimate of all the signs because they describe the human being’s own origin and social existence. The sūrah’s message is that there is no aspect of human life — from the shade that covers the body to the water from which the body was created — that is not a sign of God’s power and care.
verses.55:
> Yet they worship besides Allah what can neither benefit nor harm them. And the disbeliever always collaborates against their Lord

**The Return to Idolatry**

After the catalogue of natural signs (25:45-54), the verse returns to the sūrah's central theme: the disbelievers' worship of false gods. The transition is abrupt — from the grandeur of creation to the absurdity of idol worship — and the abruptness is deliberate. The sūrah has just showed that God controls the shade, the night, the day, the winds, the rain, the seas, and the origin of human life. Against this backdrop of total sovereignty, the worship of anything that cannot benefit or harm is not only wrong but irrational. The idols the disbelievers worship are made of the same created matter as the stones they walk on and the water they drink. They have no power over any of the phenomena the sūrah has described.

The phrase *lā yanfa'u wa-lā yaḍurru* — "that can neither benefit nor harm" — recurs throughout the Qur'an's arguments against idolatry. In 10:18 — "They worship besides Allah what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, 'These are our intercessors with Allah'" — the disbelievers' rationale is recorded: the idols serve as intercessors. In 13:16 — "Say, 'Who is Lord of the heavens and the earth?' Say, 'Allah.' Say, 'Have you then taken besides Him allies who have not even for themselves any benefit or harm?'" — the argument is stated as a challenge. Verse 25:55 adds the observation that the disbelievers continue to worship these powerless objects even after the sūrah has showed God's control over every aspect of the natural world.

**The Disbeliever as a Partisan Against God**

The second clause — *wa'l-kāfīru ʿalā Rabbihī ẓahīr* — is translated as "And the disbeliever always collaborates against their Lord," but the Arabic carries additional layers. The word *ẓahīr* can mean "helper," "ally," "supporter" — one who aids a cause. The disbeliever is described as an ally — but an ally against whom? Against God. The disbeliever is helping Satan, helping desire, helping the forces that oppose divine guidance, and the help is given at the expense of the One who created them, sustained them, and provided for them.

**The Disbeliever's Alliance Against His Own Interest**

The word *ẓahīr* (helper, ally, partisan) in 25:55 describes the disbeliever as someone who is helping a cause — but the cause is against his own Lord. The alliance is therefore self-destructive: the disbeliever is using his own power, his own resources, his own social influence to support the forces that oppose his Creator. The self-destruction is not accidental but inherent in the nature of shirk (associating others with God): to worship something besides God is to direct one's loyalty toward a target that cannot reciprocate. The idols cannot protect the disbeliever, cannot benefit him, cannot intercede for him on the Day of Judgment (25:3). The alliance with them is therefore an alliance with nothing — a partnership with entities that will abandon their worshippers at the moment of greatest need (25:17-19).
verses.56:
> And We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a deliverer of good news and a warner

**The Two Functions of Prophethood**

The verse defines the Prophet's mission in its simplest terms: *wa mā arsalnāka illā mubashshiran wa nadhīrā* — "And We have sent you only as a bearer of good news and a warner." The two nouns — *mubashshir* (bearer of good news) and *nadhīr* (warner) — name the two faces of the prophetic mission. The first face is turned toward those who believe: the Prophet brings them the good news (*bishāra*) of God's mercy, forgiveness, and the promise of Paradise. The second face is turned toward those who disbelieve: the Prophet brings them the warning (*indhār*) of God's judgment, punishment, and the reality of the fire. The two functions are not in tension; they are complementary. The good news is meaningless without the warning — because without the threat of punishment, the promise of reward has no urgency — and the warning is cruel without the good news — because without the possibility of forgiveness, the threat of punishment has no mercy.

The same pairing appears throughout the Qur'an. In 5:19 — "O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and overlooking much. There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book" — the Prophet is presented as a source of clarity. In 7:188 — "Say, 'I hold not for myself benefit or harm, except what Allah has willed. And if I knew the unseen, I could have acquired much wealth, and no harm would have touched me. I am not except a warner and a bringer of good tidings to a people who believe'" — the Prophet explicitly limits his role to these two functions. The limitation is itself a theological statement: the Prophet is not a judge, not a king, not a miracle-worker — he is a warner and a bearer of good news, and his authority extends only to the delivery of the message.

**The Word "Only" as a Limitation and an Honor**

But *illā* is also a honor: it defines the Prophet's role as exclusively this — a bearer of good news and a warner. The Prophet does not need to be anything else. His mission is complete in the delivery of good news and warning, and the delivery is the *jihād* of 25:52 — the great striving with the Quran.

**The Verse’s Relationship to the Sūrah’s Opening**

Verse 25:56 returns to the sūrah’s opening theme: the Prophet’s mission. In 25:1, the Prophet is described as “a warner to the whole world.” In 25:56, he is described as “a deliverer of good news and a warner.” (25:56)” The two descriptions bookend the sūrah’s argument: the opening names the function, the closing confirms it. Everything between — the disbelievers’ objections, the Last-Day warnings, the natural signs, the prophetic catalogues — is the content of the warning and the good news. The sūrah’s structure is thus circular: it begins with the Prophet’s mission and ends with the same mission, having showed through seventy-seven verses that the mission is necessary, the message is true, and the consequences of accepting or rejecting it are real. The Prophet’s role as mubashshir and nadhīr is not a limitation but the fulfillment of the purpose named in the very first verse.
verses.57:
> Say, “I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺, but whoever wishes, let them pursue the Way to their Lord.”

**The Prophet's Disinterestedness**

The verse records a statement the Prophet is commanded to make: *qul mā as'alukum ʿalayhi min ajrin* — "Say, 'I do not ask you for any reward for it.'" The declaration of disinterestedness is one of the Qur'an's most consistent themes in describing the prophetic mission. The same statement appears in 26:109, 127, 145, 164, and 180 — each time attributed to a different prophet (Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, Shu'ayb) — and in 34:47 — "Say, 'Whatever reward I have asked of you — it is yours. My reward is only from Allah.'" The repetition across prophetic history establishes a principle: the prophetic mission is not a commercial enterprise. The Prophet does not profit from the delivery of the message. He does not seek wealth, status, political power, or social approval. He seeks nothing from his audience except their engagement with the message, and the engagement is for their benefit, not his.

The declaration serves a practical purpose in the sūrah's argument. The disbelievers had accused the Prophet of pursuing personal goals through his message — wealth, leadership, a share of the Quraysh's power. The declaration in 25:57 answers these accusations directly: the Prophet asks for nothing. The absence of a demand for reward is itself evidence of sincerity: a fabricator would seek compensation for his effort; a true messenger seeks nothing but the delivery of the truth. The disinterestedness is therefore not merely a moral quality but an argument — it is one of the proofs that the Prophet's mission is genuine. The second half of the verse — *illā man shā'a a yattakhidha ilā Rabbihi sabīlā* — offers the audience an alternative: "but whoever wishes, let them take a way unto his Lord." The word *sabīl* (Way, path) appears here for the thirteenth time in the sūrah, maintaining the thread that runs through the entire chapter. The Way is available; the choice to walk it is offered; and the offer is made without compulsion. The word *man shā'a* ("whoever wishes") introduces radical freedom: the choice belongs completely to the individual.

**The Verse’s Place in the Sūrah’s Argument**

Verse 25:57 follows the Prophet’s role definition (25:56) and precedes the command to trust in God (25:58). The sequence — mission, disinterestedness, trust — defines the Prophet’s posture in the world: he delivers the message without asking for anything in return, and he relies on God for the outcome. The disinterestedness is not indifference; it is the Prophet’s way of saying that the message belongs to God, not to him, and the reward for delivering it belongs to God, not to the audience. The Prophet’s only request is that the audience consider the Way — the path to their Lord — and the request is made without pressure, without condition, and without threat. The sūrah’s structure thus moves from the Prophet’s selflessness (25:57) to his trust in God (25:58), and the movement defines the prophetic character: a person who gives without expecting and trusts without seeing, who delivers the message and leaves the outcome to the One who sent it.

The Prophet asks nothing (25:57); God compels nothing (2:256: “There is no compulsion in religion”); and the individual is left to decide for themselves.
verses.58:
> Put your trust in the Ever-Living, Who never dies, and glorify His praises. Sufficient is He as All-Aware of the sins of His servants

The verse addresses the Prophet with a command: *wa tawakkal ʿalā'l-ḥayyī'lladhī lā yamūtu* — "And put your trust in the Ever-Living, Who does not die." The word *tawakkal* (to trust, to rely upon, to place one's affairs in the hands of) names a specific form of faith: not merely belief in God's existence but active reliance on God's care. The Prophet is commanded to trust — to release his grip on his own plans and strategies and place the outcome of his mission in God's hands.

The description of God as *al-ḥayy* (the Ever-Living) is paired with the negation *alladhī lā yamūtu* (Who does not die). The Prophet's opponents — the disbelievers of Makkah, their idols, their social structures — will all die. The attribute *al-ḥayy* appears prominently in 2:255 — "Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence" — the verse known as Āyat al-Kursī, the most recited verse in the Qur'an.

**Glorifying God's Praises**

The pairing of trust and glorification appears in other Qur'anic passages. In 3:173 — "Those to whom people said, 'Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them.' But it increased them in faith, and they said, 'Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best disposer of affairs'" — the believers respond to threat with trust. In 33:41-42 — "O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance and exalt Him morning and evening" — the command to remember God is given in the context of the Prophet's mission. The consistency of the pattern — trust and glorify, rely and praise — defines the believer's posture in the world: not passive but active, not resigned but confident, not silent but vocal in the declaration of God's greatness.

**Sufficient as All-Aware**

The verse closes with *wa kafā bihi bi-dhunūbi ʿibādihī khabīrā* — "Sufficient is He as All-Aware of the sins of His servants." The word *kafā* (enough) echoes 25:31 — "Sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and Helper" — and establishes a refrain: God is enough. The Prophet does not need the disbelievers' approval (25:31), does not need their reward (25:57), and does not need their help. God is enough — as Guide, as Helper, as Judge, and as Witness. The word *khabīr* (All-Aware, fully informed) names God's knowledge of the sins of His servants. The combination of sufficiency and awareness is both a comfort and a warning: God is enough for the Prophet, and God knows what the disbelievers do. The awareness is total — no sin is hidden, no mockery is unseen, and no rejection is unrecorded. The Day of Judgment will make visible what God already knows, and the knowledge is the ground of the justice that the Day will deliver.
verses.59:
> ˹He is˺ the One Who created the heavens and the earth and everything in between in six Days, then established Himself on the Throne. ˹He is˺ the Most Compassionate! Ask ˹none other than˺ the All-Knowledgeable about Himself

**Creation in Six Days**

The verse returns to the theme of divine creation that has run through the sūrah since 25:2: *alladhī khalaqa's-samāwāti wa'l-arḍa wa mā baynahumā fī sittati ayyām* — "The One who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days." The creation in six days is mentioned in multiple Qur'anic passages — 7:54, 10:3, 11:7, 32:4, 50:38. 57:4 — each time as an assertion of God's sovereign creative power. The number six is not arbitrary; it is the number the Qur'an consistently assigns to the act of creation, and the commentators debate whether the "days" are literal twenty-four-hour periods or longer epochs. Al-Rāzī notes that the question is essentially imponderable — God could have created in an instant or in a million years, and the choice of "six days" is a divine decision that human beings cannot fully understand. The point is not the duration but the fact: the creation was deliberate, ordered, and complete.

**The Throne and Divine Sovereignty**

The Throne (*ʿarsh*) in the Qur'anic cosmology is the greatest of God's creations — the canopy that encompasses the entire cosmos, above the heavens and the earth. Its mention in 25:59 is not incidental; it establishes the hierarchy of creation. Everything below the Throne — the heavens, the earth, and what is between them — was created in six days. The Throne itself was created before or alongside them, and God's establishment upon it marks the completion of creation and the beginning of divine governance. The message is sovereignty: the God who created everything rules everything, and the rule is exercised from the position of absolute authority.

**Al-Raḥmān: Ask About Him**

The verse ends with a striking instruction: *fa-s'al bihi khabīrā* — "So ask about Him, the All-Aware" or "Ask about Him, One who is aware." The instruction can be read in two ways. First, "Ask about the Most Compassionate" — the Prophet is directed to seek knowledge about God from the One who knows, that is, from God Himself. Second, "Ask about it" — the Prophet is directed to ask about the creation of the heavens and the earth from someone who is knowledgeable, that is, from God or from the scholars who understand such matters. Al-Rāzī notes that the first reading is more likely if the instruction is addressed to the Prophet, since the Prophet would not need to ask a human being about God. The instruction is therefore a command to seek knowledge of God from God — to turn to revelation, to prayer, to the direct relationship between the servant and the Lord. The Most Compassionate is the subject of the question, and the answer comes from the One who knows Himself best.
verses.60:
> When it is said to them, “Prostrate to the Most Compassionate,” they ask ˹in disgust˺, “What is ‘the Most Compassionate’? Will we prostrate to whatever you order us to?” And it only drives them farther away

**The Refusal to Prostrate**

The verse describes the disbelievers' response to the command to prostrate before *al-Raḥmān* (the Most Compassionate): *wa idhā qīla lahumu'sjudū li'l-Raḥmāni qālū wa mā'r-Raḥmān* — "When it is said to them, 'Prostrate to the Most Compassionate,' they say, 'What is the Most Compassionate?'" The question is not genuine inquiry but contempt. The disbelievers are not asking for information; they are expressing their refusal to acknowledge a name for God that they do not recognize. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the pre-Islamic Arabs were familiar with the name *Allāh* but not with the name *al-Raḥmān*. At the signing of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Quraysh negotiators objected when the Prophet instructed that the treaty be written "In the Name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful," saying they knew neither of those names. The objection was not theological but cultural: the name *al-Raḥmān* was unfamiliar, and unfamiliarity was treated as illegitimacy.

The disbelievers' question — *a-nasjudu limā ta'murunā* — "Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?" — adds a layer of defiance. The disbelievers are not only refusing the command; they are questioning the authority behind it. The implicit accusation is that the Prophet is inventing a god — imposing a name that their tradition does not support, demanding worship of a being they do not recognize. The refusal is therefore not a theological disagreement about the nature of God but a social rebellion against the Prophet's authority to redefine the terms of worship. The disbelievers' gods have names they know, rituals they inherited, and a place in their social order. *Al-Raḥmān* has none of these — and the absence, for the disbelievers, is reason enough to refuse.

**The Name al-Raḥmān and Its Significance**

The name *al-Raḥmān* (the Most Compassionate) is the intensive form of *raḥmah* (mercy, compassion), and it carries a force that exceeds the more common *al-Raḥīm* (the Most Merciful). *Al-Raḥmān* names the quality of compassion that pervades all of creation — the compassion that sends rain (25:48), that creates night for rest (25:47), that extends the shade (25:45), and that provides for every living thing (25:49). The sūrah has spent the last fifteen verses demonstrating this compassion through the catalogue of natural signs, and the command to prostrate before *al-Raḥmān* is the logical conclusion of the demonstration: the One who does all of this deserves prostration.

**The Verse’s Role in the Sūrah’s Argument**

Verse 25:60 completes the section that began with the description of creation in 25:59. The God who created the heavens and the earth and established Himself on the Throne is the same God the disbelievers refuse to prostrate to. The connection between the two verses is the sūrah’s way of saying: the God who has the power to create the cosmos deserves prostration, and the refusal to prostrate is the most extreme form of the arrogance (istikbār) named in 25:21. The disbelievers’ question — “What is the Most Compassionate?” — is, after fifteen verses of natural signs (25:45-59), an act of willful ignorance. The sūrah does not answer the question because the question is not genuine; it is the disbelievers’ final refusal, the last barrier between them and the truth, and the barrier is made not of stone or water but of will.
verses.61:
> Blessed is the One Who has placed constellations in the sky, as well as a ˹radiant˺ lamp and a luminous moon

**The Return of Tabāraka**

The verse opens with *tabāraka* — "Blessed is" — the same word that opened the sūrah in 25:1. The repetition creates a structural frame: the sūrah begins and ends its catalogue of signs with the same declaration of divine praise. The word *tabāraka* carries the sense of continuous increase in goodness, and its appearance in 25:61, after sixty verses of argument, warning, and evidence, returns the reader to the starting point. Everything that has been said — the disbelievers' objections, the fire, the garden, the prophetic catalogue, the natural signs — is placed under the umbrella of a God whose nature is blessing. The sūrah's argument is not made from a position of anger but from a position of praise: the God who warns is the God who blesses, and the blessing is visible in the sky above.

The specific signs mentioned — constellations (*burūj*), a lamp (*sirāj*), and a luminous moon (*nūr*) — are the most visible features of the night sky. The constellations mark the fixed patterns against which the celestial bodies move; the lamp is the sun, which provides the primary light; and the moon reflects that light in a softer, gentler form. The word *burūj* (constellations) appears elsewhere in 15:16 and 85:1, each time as a marker of God's creative power.

**The Sun as a Lamp and the Moon as Light**

The distinction between the sun (*sirāj*, lamp) and the moon (*nūr*, light) is both physical and theological. The sun produces its own light through nuclear fusion; the moon reflects the sun's light. The Qur'anic vocabulary captures this distinction: a *sirāj* is a source of illumination, a burning lamp; a *nūr* is a derived light, a reflection. The distinction appears in 71:16 — "And made the moon a light among them. Made the sun a lamp" — and in 78:13 — "And made a blazing lamp." The consistency of the vocabulary across the Qur'an establishes a cosmological framework in which the sun and the moon are not equals but complementary: one produces, the other receives; one burns, the other glows. The theological implication is that creation is hierarchical: some things are sources, and some things are reflections, and the hierarchy is part of the design.

**The Verse's Role in the Sūrah's Final Sign Catalogue**

Verse 25:61 opens the sūrah's final section — a brief catalogue of cosmic and natural signs that prepares for the closing address to the Prophet in 25:77. The section moves from the sky (25:61) to the alternation of day and night (25:62) to the character of God's true servants (25:63-76) to the Prophet's final declaration (25:77). The movement is from the cosmic to the moral, from the signs in the heavens to the signs in human character. The sūrah's method is consistent: it shows God's power through the observable world and then shows what that power demands of the human beings who observe it. The constellations, the lamp, and the moon are the last natural signs in the sūrah, and they prepare the reader for the description of the servants of the Most Compassionate — the people who observe the signs and respond with the humility, prayer, and generosity that the signs call for.

The Qur'an acknowledges this function in 6:97 — "And it is He who has made the stars for you, that you may be guided by them through the darkness of the land and sea" — and in 16:16 — "and landmarks.
verses.62:
> And He is the One Who causes the day and the night to alternate, ˹as a sign˺ for whoever desires to be mindful or to be grateful

The verse describes the alternation of day and night — *yukhlifu bayna'l-layli wa'n-nahār* — as a sign (*āyah*) for two kinds of people: whoever desires to be mindful (*yattadhakkar*) and whoever desires to be grateful (*yashkur*). The person who observes the alternation of day and night and reflects on its cause — who recognizes that the transition from darkness to light and back again is not random but designed — practices *tadhakkur* (mindfulness). The person who then acknowledges the Designer and thanks Him for the provision of time — time to work, time to rest, time to worship — practices *shukr* (gratitude).

The word *yattadhakkar* (to be mindful, to remember, to reflect) is the same root as *tadhakkur* in 25:50, where the distribution of rain is described as a sign "so they may be mindful." The repetition connects the two passages: the rain is a sign that invites mindfulness. The alternation of day and night is a sign that invites mindfulness. The sūrah's catalogue of signs — rain, shade, night, day, wind, seas, constellations — is unified by the single purpose of *tadhakkur*: every sign exists to provoke the same response, and the response is the beginning of faith.

**The Day and Night as a Framework for Worship**

In 17:78 — "Establish prayer at the sun's decline until the darkness of the night, and recite at dawn — indeed, the recitation of dawn is witnessed" — the Qur'an specifies the times of prayer by reference to the movement of the sun and the onset of darkness. The alternation of day and night is thus the temporal framework within which the Muslim community organizes its worship, and the framework is itself a sign of God's design. The person who prays at the appointed times is responding to the sign in the most direct way possible: not merely observing the alternation but using it, not merely being grateful but expressing the gratitude in action.

**The Verse's Placement Before the Servants of the Compassionate**

Verse 25:62 serves as a bridge between the natural signs (25:61) and the description of God's true servants (25:63-76). The alternation of day and night is the last of the cosmic signs, and the two qualities it is designed to produce — mindfulness and gratitude — are the qualities that define the servants of the Most Compassionate. The servants described in 25:63-76 are people who have responded to the signs correctly: they walk humbly (25:63), they pray at night (25:64), they ask God to protect them from Hell (25:65-66), they spend moderately (25:67), and they avoid the sins of idolatry, murder, and fornication (25:68). Every quality they have is a response to the signs the sūrah has described: the humility comes from recognizing God's power in the natural world; the prayer comes from recognizing God's generosity in the provision of sustenance; the moderation comes from recognizing God's design in the balance of creation. The servants of the Compassionate are the living proof that the signs work — for those who are willing.
verses.63:
> The ˹true˺ servants of the Most Compassionate are those who walk on the earth humbly, and when the foolish address them ˹improperly˺, they only respond with peace

**The Opening Portrait of the Servants**

The verse introduces the sūrah's most sustained portrait of ideal human character: *ʿibādu'l-Raḥmān* — "the servants of the Most Compassionate." The name *al-Raḥmān* (the Most Compassionate) connects this portrait to the sūrah's earlier uses of the same name: in 25:26, true sovereignty belongs to the Most Compassionate on the Day of Judgment. In 25:59, God is described as the Most Compassionate who created the heavens and the earth; and in 25:60, the disbelievers refuse to prostrate to the Most Compassionate. The servants of the Most Compassionate are the human response to the divine attribute: they are the people who recognize the compassion behind creation and model their lives on it.

The portrait that begins here and extends through 25:76 is one of the Qur'an's most celebrated passages. It has been used as a template for Muslim character formation for fourteen centuries, and its influence on Islamic ethics is incalculable. The portrait does not describe a theoretical ideal but a lived reality: the servants walk, speak, pray, spend, and interact with others in specific ways that are recognizable and replicable. The sūrah's method is not to prescribe abstract principles but to describe concrete behaviors, and the behaviors together constitute a character that is both spiritual and practical.

**Humility in Walking**

The specification that the servants walk "on the earth" (*ʿalā'l-arḍ*) is significant. The earth is the stage on which human life is performed, and the servants' humility is displayed on that stage — in public, in the presence of others, in the ordinary interactions of daily life. The humility is not private; it is visible. The servants do not retreat to monasteries or hide in caves; they walk among people, and their walking is itself a sign — a sign that the one who recognizes God does not need to assert dominance over other human beings. The contrast with 25:21 is the sūrah's way of showing the two modes of being: the disbelievers walk with arrogance and exceed all limits; the servants walk with humility and maintain all limits. The contrast is the Criterion (25:1) in action.

**The Connection to the Sūrah's Earlier Descriptions of Mockery**

The portrait of the servants' response to the foolish connects directly to the sūrah's earlier descriptions of the disbelievers' mockery. In 25:41, the disbelievers see the Prophet and make fun of him. In 25:42, they claim he nearly led them astray from their gods. In 25:60, they respond to the command to prostrate with contempt. The servants of the Compassionate are the mirror image of the disbelievers: where the disbelievers mock, the servants say peace; where the disbelievers demand, the servants give; where the disbelievers are arrogant, the servants are humble. The servants are what the disbelievers are not, and the contrast is the sūrah's way of showing what the Criterion (25:1) produces when it is accepted rather than rejected.

The portrait also connects to the broader Qur'anic ethic of patience (*ṣabr*). In 41:34-35 — "Good and evil are not equal. But this cannot be attained except by those who are patient" — the Qur'an describes the transformation that patience produces: the enemy becomes a friend.
verses.64:
> ˹They are˺ those who spend ˹a good portion of˺ the night, prostrating themselves and standing before their Lord

**The Night Vigil as the Mark of Devotion**

The verse describes the second quality of the servants of the Most Compassionate: their practice of spending the night in prayer — *alladhīna yabītūna li-Rabbihim sujjadan wa qiyāmān* — "those who pass the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing." The word *yabītūna* (they pass the night) specifies the time: these are not prayers performed in the convenience of daylight but in the solitude and silence of the night, when the world sleeps and the worshipper is alone with God. The two postures — *sujūd* (prostration) and *qiyām* (standing) — describe the physical acts of Islamic prayer: standing upright in recitation and bowing low in submission. The combination covers the full range of prayer's physical expression: the worshipper stands before God in attention and falls before God in humility.

The practice of night prayer (*tahajjud* or *qiyām al-layl*) is one of the most emphasized acts of devotion in the Qur'an. In 17:79 — "And rise from sleep during the night, as an extra offering of your own, so that your Lord may raise you to a praised station" — the Prophet is specifically commanded to pray at night. In 73:1-4 — "O you who wraps himself in clothing, arise to pray the night, except for a little" — the same command is given with even more urgency. The night prayer is not obligatory for the general community, but it is the mark of those whose devotion goes beyond the minimum. The servants of the Compassionate are identified by this practice because it reveals the depth of their relationship with God: they give God the time that is most precious — the hours of rest — and the sacrifice is the proof of their sincerity.

**The Verse's Connection to the Servants' Portrait**

Verse 25:64 continues the portrait that began in 25:63. The first quality was humility in walking and patience with the foolish; the second quality is devotion in prayer. The two are related: the humility that characterizes the servants' public life is rooted in the submission that characterizes their private worship. A person who spends the night prostrating before God will not walk through the day with arrogance; a person who stands before God in the darkness will not respond to the foolish with anything but peace. The night prayer is the source, and the daytime virtues are the fruit. The sūrah's portrait of the servants is therefore not a random collection of virtues but a coherent character: the person who worships at night is the person who walks humbly by day, and the person who walks humbly by day is the person who says peace to the foolish. The character is whole, and the wholeness comes from the single source: submission to the Most Compassionate.
verses.65:
> ˹They are˺ those who pray, “Our Lord! Keep the punishment of Hell away from us, for its punishment is indeed unrelenting

**The Prayer That Defines the Servants**

The verse records the servants' own words: *wa'lladhīna yaqūlūna Rabbanā'ṣrif ʿannā ʿadhāba jahannama* — "and those who say, 'Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell.'" The prayer is addressed to God as *Rabbanā* (our Lord), a possessive form that expresses intimacy and dependence. The servants do not address God from a position of merit or entitlement; they address Him as children address a parent — with need, with vulnerability, with the recognition that their safety depends on His mercy. The word *aṣrif* (avert, turn away) is a request for protection, not a claim of immunity. The servants do not say "we deserve to be spared"; they say "spare us," and the request acknowledges that without God's intervention, they have no defense against the punishment.

**The Theology of Fear in the Servants' Portrait**

The servants' prayer in 25:65-66 introduces fear as a component of their spiritual character. They fear Hell — not abstractly but specifically, not theoretically but with the kind of concrete awareness that produces prayer. This fear is not the opposite of love; it is its companion. The servants love God (expressed through their worship) and fear God (expressed through their prayer for protection), and the two together constitute the complete relationship. The Qur'an consistently pairs fear and love as the two wings of faith: "Call upon Him in fear and hope" (7:56); "They used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear" (21:90). The servants of the Compassionate are people who have not chosen one wing over the other; they fly with both.

The placement of this prayer after the night vigil (25:64) is significant. The servants who spend the night in prostration and standing are the same people who pray for protection from Hell. The night prayer is the context; the fear of Hell is the content. The servants' worship is not joyful only; it is also fearful. The night is not spent in celebration alone but in supplication, in the acknowledgment that the one who worships God most deeply is also the one who fears God most honestly. The relationship between devotion and fear is not paradoxical but causal: the closer one draws to God, the more one understands the gravity of sin, and the more one understands the gravity of sin, the more one prays for protection from its consequence.
verses.66:
> It is certainly an evil place to settle and reside.”

The verse completes the servants' prayer that began in 25:65: *innahā sā'at mustaqarran wa muqāmān* — "Truly it is an evil place to settle and abode." The two words — *mustaqarr* (settlement, dwelling) and *muqām* (abode, place of residence) — are the same words used in 25:24 to describe the righteous in Paradise: "the residents of Paradise will have the best settlement (*mustaqarr*) and the finest place to rest (*maqīl*)." The verbal echo between the two verses is deliberate: the servants of the Compassionate, in their prayer for protection from Hell, use the same vocabulary that the sūrah used for Paradise.

The servants do not describe Hell's fire, its chains, its narrow places, or its sounds — all of which the sūrah has already described in 25:12-14.

**The Rhetorical Power of the Verse's Brevity**

Verse 25:66 is among the shortest verses in the sūrah, consisting of only six words in Arabic. The brevity is itself a rhetorical device. After the extended description of Hell in 25:12-14 — the fire, the smoke, the narrow place, the cry — the servants' verdict is delivered in the most compressed form possible. The compression is effective: the servants do not need to repeat the details because the details have already been established. All they need to say is *sā'at* — "evil" — and the reader's memory fills in the rest. The brevity also conveys the servants' certainty: they do not hedge, do not qualify, do not soften the verdict. Hell is an evil place to settle, and the statement is final.

The verse's position as the conclusion of the servants' prayer adds to its force. The prayer began in 25:65 with the request for protection and the description of the punishment as *gharām* (unrelenting). The prayer closes in 25:66 with the verdict on Hell as a dwelling. The structure — request, description, verdict — is the structure of a legal argument: the servants present their case (we need protection), the evidence (the punishment is permanent), and the conclusion (Hell is an evil place to live). The argument is directed to God, who needs no persuasion, but the argument's structure is for the reader's benefit: it shows that the servants' fear of Hell is not emotional but reasoned, not irrational but grounded in the sūrah's own descriptions.

**The Contrast With the Garden**

The sūrah's structural pairing of 25:66 with 25:24 creates one of its most powerful contrasts. In 25:24, the righteous have "the best settlement and the finest place to rest." In 25:66, the condemned have "an evil place to settle and reside." The same nouns — settlement and dwelling — describe both outcomes, and the adjective is the only difference: best vs. Evil. The contrast is the sūrah's way of presenting the two options as a single choice with a single variable: where will you settle? The answer depends on what you do in this life — whether you walk humbly (25:63), pray at night (25:64), ask for protection from Hell (25:65), and live by the principles the sūrah describes. The choice is binary, the vocabulary is identical, and the difference is the life that precedes the settlement.
verses.67:
> ˹They are˺ those who spend neither wastefully nor stingily, but moderately in between

**The Middle Way in Spending**

The verse describes the servants' relationship to wealth: *wa'lladhīna idhā anfaqū lam yusrifū wa lam yaqturū wa kāna bayna dhālika qawāmān* — "and those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor miserly. Maintain a middle way between them." The word *isrāf* (extravagance, wastefulness) names one extreme; the word *iqṭār* (miserliness, stinginess) names the other; and the word *qawām* (middle, balanced, upright) names the position between them. The servants are people who have found the balance — the point at which spending is generous enough to fulfill its purpose and restrained enough to preserve its sustainability.

The concept of the middle way (*wasaṭ*) is one of the Qur'an's most fundamental ethical principles. In 2:143 — "And thus We have made you a middle community" — the same root is used to describe the Muslim community as a whole. The middle way is not mediocrity; it is the point of maximum effectiveness, the position from which the most good can be done over the longest period. The extravagant person gives too much and soon has nothing left to give; the miserly person gives too little and accumulates what benefits no one. The servant of the Compassionate gives enough — enough to be generous, enough to be sustainable, and enough to maintain the capacity to give again.

**The Verse's Connection to the Sūrah's Earlier Warnings Against Excess**

The mention of *isrāf* (wastefulness) in 25:67 connects to the Qur'an's broader warnings against excess. In 7:31 — "Eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who commit excess" — the same word is used in the context of food and drink. In 17:26-27 — "And do not make your hand chained to your neck or extend it completely... Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils" — extravagance is linked to moral corruption. The servants of the Compassionate are the opposite of the wasteful: they are measured, balanced, and deliberate in their spending. The measurement is not calculation but character — it flows naturally from the humility (25:63) and the devotion (25:64) that define their relationship with God.

**The Practical Nature of the Servants' Portrait**

Verse 25:67 adds a practical dimension to the portrait that has been building since 25:63. The servants walk humbly, respond to the foolish with peace, pray at night, ask for protection from Hell, and now spend moderately. The portrait moves from the spiritual (humility, prayer) to the practical (spending), and the movement shows that the servants' character is not limited to private worship but extends to public conduct. The servants of the Compassionate are not monks; they are members of society who earn, spend, and interact with others.
verses.68:
> ˹They are˺ those who do not invoke any other god besides Allah, nor take a ˹human˺ life—made sacred by Allah—except with ˹legal˺ right, nor commit fornication. And whoever does ˹any of˺ this will face the penalty

**The Three Prohibitions**

The verse names three prohibitions that define the moral boundaries of the servants of the Compassionate: *shirk* (associating others with God), murder (taking a life sanctified by God without right), and *zinā* (fornication or adultery). The three are grouped together because they represent violations of the three fundamental relationships in human existence: the relationship with God (*shirk*), the relationship with other human beings (murder), and the relationship with the family and social order (fornication). The servants of the Compassionate are people who maintain all three relationships in their proper form: they worship God alone, they respect human life, and they preserve the integrity of the sexual and familial order.

The prohibition of *shirk* — "those who do not invoke any other god besides Allah" — returns the sūrah to its opening theme. The Criterion (25:1) was sent down to distinguish truth from falsehood, and the primary falsehood is the association of other beings with God. The servants of the Compassionate are the people who have accepted the Criterion and live by it: their worship is directed to God alone, and their refusal to invoke other gods is the foundation of their character. The prohibition of murder — "nor take a life made sacred by Allah except with right" — affirms the inviolability of human life. The word *ḥaram* (sacred, inviolable) describes the status of human life in God's law: it cannot be taken except in the specific circumstances that the law permits (capital punishment for capital crimes, self-defense in the face of aggression). The prohibition of fornication — "nor commit fornication" — protects the integrity of the family, the social unit that the sūrah described in 25:54 as divinely designed through kinship and marriage.

**The Sacredness of Human Life**

In 5:32 — "Whoever kills a soul — unless for a soul or for corruption in the land — it is as if he had slain mankind completely. And whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind completely" — the value of a single life is equated with the value of all humanity.

**The Verse's Role in the Servants' Portrait**

Verse 25:68 is the moral center of the servants' portrait. The portrait has described their virtues — humility (25:63), prayer (25:64-66), moderation (25:67) — and now it names the vices they avoid. The combination of positive qualities and negative prohibitions creates a complete picture: the servants are defined not only by what they do but by what they refuse to do. The refusal is as important as the action, because the prohibitions protect the foundations — faith, life, family — without which the virtues cannot stand. A person who is humble but idolatrous is humble in the service of a falsehood; a person who prays but murders is praying with blood on their hands; a person who spends moderately but commits fornication is moderating their wealth while violating their integrity. The prohibitions are the guardrails that keep the virtues on track, and the servants of the Compassionate are people who honor both.
verses.69:
> Their punishment will be multiplied on the Day of Judgment, and they will remain in it forever, in disgrace

**The Multiplication of Punishment**

The verse describes the consequence for those who violate the three prohibitions of 25:68: *yudāʿaf lahu'l-ʿadhābu yawma'l-qiyāmati* — "the punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Judgment." The word *yudāʿaf* (doubled, multiplied) appears in other Qur'anic Last-Day passages: in 11:20 — "For those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those will be the companions of the Fire; they will abide in it. For them the punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be reprieved" — and in 33:30 — "And whoever of you commits immorality, We will multiply the punishment for her, and that is easy for Allah." The multiplication is not arbitrary; it is proportional to the severity of the sin. The violations named in 25:68 — *shirk*, murder, fornication — are among the gravest sins in the Qur'anic moral framework, and the punishment corresponds to their gravity.

**The Reversal of the Disbelievers' Expectations**

The multiplication of punishment is also a reversal of the disbelievers' expectations. In 25:21, the disbelievers said: "We have never heard of this in any previous faith. This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but a fabrication." Their dismissal of the punishment was based on the assumption that no consequence would follow from their disbelief. Verse 25:69 corrects the assumption: the consequence not only exists but is multiplied. The multiplication is the sūrah's answer to the disbelievers' dismissal: the punishment is not diminished by their disbelief; it is increased. The person who denies the punishment receives more of it, and the "more" is the justice of God — the justice that responds to rejection with severity and to acceptance with mercy.

The word *muhanān* (disgraced, humiliated) also carries overtones of the social humiliation that the disbelievers inflicted on others during their lives. The disbelievers of Makkah humiliated the weak, the poor, and the enslaved — people like Bilāl, ʿAmmār, and Sumayyah, who were tortured for their faith. The word *muhanān* in 25:69 reverses the social order: in the Hereafter, the humiliators become the humiliated, and the humiliated become the honored. The reversal is the sūrah's way of demonstrating that the social order of this world is not the final order — that the hierarchies of power, wealth. Status that the disbelievers relied on will be overturned on the Day of Judgment, and the people who were at the bottom in this life will be at the top in the next.
verses.70:
> As for those who repent, believe, and do good deeds, they are the ones whose evil deeds Allah will change into good deeds. For Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

The verse introduces an exception to the punishment described in 25:69: *illā man tāba wa āmana wa ʿamila ʿāmalan ṣāliḥan* — "except for those who repent, believe. Do good deeds." The exception is significant because it follows the most severe warning in the sūrah — the doubled punishment, the eternity of disgrace — and shows that the punishment is not inevitable. The door of repentance remains open, even for those who have committed the gravest sins (*shirk*, murder, fornication in 25:68).

Al-Ṭabarī records that this verse was revealed in response to the anxiety of some idolaters who were inclined to embrace Islam but felt that their previous sins — the very sins listed in 25:68 — could never be forgiven.

**The Connection to the Sūrah's Earlier Forgiveness Passages**

The promise of forgiveness in 25:70 connects to the sūrah's earlier references to divine mercy. In 25:10, God describes the disbelievers' objection — "If only the Compassionate had a son, I would be the foremost in worship" — and the implication is that God's mercy is available to anyone who turns to Him. In 25:65-66, the servants pray for protection from Hell, and the prayer is itself an act of repentance — an acknowledgment of their dependence on God's mercy. Verse 25:70 generalizes the principle: not only the servants but anyone who repents sincerely can receive the transformation of evil into good. The verse is therefore the sūrah's most inclusive statement of divine mercy — inclusive not in the sense that everyone is forgiven regardless of their actions but in the sense that everyone is eligible for forgiveness if they meet the conditions. The conditions are clear, the mercy is real, and the transformation is guaranteed for those who fulfill the conditions.

The three conditions of 25:70 — repentance, faith, and righteous action — are not arbitrary but structurally necessary. Repentance without faith is regret without direction: the person feels bad about what they have done but has no new framework within which to build a different life. Faith without righteous action is belief without expression: the person affirms the truth but does not live by it. And righteous action without repentance is effort without foundation: the person does good deeds but carries the weight of the old sins without having turned away from them. The three together form a complete system: repentance clears the ground, faith plants the seed, and righteous action cultivates the harvest. The servants of the Compassionate have completed all three steps, and the completion is what earns them the transformation of their evil deeds into good. The sūrah's promise is not a free gift but a reward for a process — a process that begins with the hardest step (admitting the sin) and ends with the most productive step (doing good).

Verse 25:70 is structurally positioned between the punishment of the condemned (25:69) and the continuation of the servants' portrait (25:71-76).
verses.71:
> And whoever repents and does good has truly turned to Allah properly

**The Linguistic Depth of Matabān**

The word *matabān* deserves particular attention. It is the intensive form (*faʿāl*) of *tawbah*, and the intensification suggests that the repentance is not ordinary but extraordinary — not a simple apology but a profound transformation. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the *faʿāl* pattern in Arabic often indicates a sustained or intensive quality: *ṣawwāb* means "very accurate," *jawwād* means "very generous," and *matabān* means "very repentant" or "thoroughly turned." The servants' repentance is not a momentary regret but a sustained commitment, a reorientation that lasts for the rest of their lives. The word *matabān* thus names not only the act of repentance but the quality of the life that follows: the servants who turn to God do not turn back.

The distinction between ordinary repentance and *matabān* is relevant to the sūrah's overall message. The disbelievers have been warned throughout the sūrah — through Last-Day descriptions, prophetic examples, and natural signs — and some of them may have been moved to regret.

**The Verse's Placement as a Bridge**

The placement of 25:71 immediately before the continuation of the servants' portrait (25:72-76) creates a structural bridge. The sūrah has described the servants' virtues (25:63-68), the punishment for those who violate the servants' principles (25:69), the possibility of repentance (25:70-71), and now returns to the servants' character (25:72-76). The message is that the servants are not a closed category; anyone can join them through repentance. The door is open, the conditions are clear, and the reward is guaranteed. The sūrah's portrait of the servants is therefore not a description of a spiritual elite but a description of what every human being can become — if they choose to turn. The bridge of 25:71 connects the warning (25:69) to the hope (25:72-76), and the connection is the sūrah's final gift to its audience: the chance to change.
verses.72:
> ˹They are˺ those who do not bear false witness, and when they come across falsehood, they pass ˹it˺ by with dignity

**The Gravity of False Witnessing in Islamic Ethics**

The connection between false witnessing and moral corruption is deeply rooted in Islamic ethics. The Prophet is reported to have said: "Shall I not tell you of the greatest of the major sins? Associating partners with God, and disobeying parents." He was reclining, then sat up and said: "And false testimony." The repetition of the hadith — the Prophet's physical repositioning to emphasize the gravity of the sin — underlines the importance of truthfulness in the Islamic moral framework. False witnessing is not only a lie; it is an assault on the social order, a corruption of the judicial process, and a betrayal of the trust that human beings place in one another. The servants of the Compassionate refuse to participate in this corruption, and the refusal is a defining feature of their character.

The placement of false witnessing alongside the prohibitions of 25:68 (*shirk*, murder, fornication) reveals the sūrah's understanding of what constitutes a fundamental sin. The three prohibitions of 25:68 violate the relationships with God, with other human beings, and with the family. False witnessing violates the relationship with truth itself — the foundation upon which all other relationships rest. A society in which false witnessing is tolerated is a society in which no contract is reliable, no testimony is trustworthy, and no justice is possible. The servants' refusal to bear false witness is therefore not merely a personal virtue but a social service: by maintaining their commitment to truth, they protect the social fabric that holds their community together. The second quality is the servants' response when they encounter falsehood: *wa idhā marrū bi'l-laghw marrū kirāmān* — "and when they pass by falsehood, they pass by with dignity." The word *laghw* (idle talk, vanity, purposeless speech) describes the kind of falsehood the servants encounter in daily life — gossip, mockery, pointless argument. The general noise of a society that does not prioritize truth.

In 17:70 — "We have honored (*karramnā*) the children of Adam" — the same root describes God's gift of dignity to all human beings. The servants of the Compassionate live out that dignity: they do not lower themselves to the level of the foolish (25:63), they do not participate in the falsehoods of their society, and they pass by what is beneath them with the quiet assurance of people who know their worth.

**The Practical Ethics of the Servants' Portrait**

Verse 25:72 adds a practical ethical dimension to the portrait. The servants are not only spiritually devoted (praying at night, asking for protection from Hell) but morally disciplined (refusing false testimony, passing by idle talk with dignity). The combination of spiritual devotion and moral discipline is the sūrah's definition of the complete human being: one who worships God in private and maintains integrity in public. The servants of the Compassionate are not monks who withdraw from society; they are citizens who engage with society on their own terms — terms set by the Criterion (25:1) and maintained by the character the Criterion produces.

The portrait, taken as a whole from 25:63 to 25:76, is one of the Qur'an's most comprehensive character sketches. Each verse adds a new dimension: humility in walking, patience with the foolish, night prayer, fear of Hell, moderation in spending, avoidance of the gravest sins, refusal of false witnessing, and dignified passing by falsehood. The dimensions together create a person who is fully integrated — a person whose inner life (prayer, fear, repentance) matches their outer conduct (walking, speaking, spending, witnessing). The integration is the servants' greatest achievement, and the sūrah presents it as the model for all believers. The Criterion (25:1) was sent down to distinguish truth from falsehood, and the servants are the people who have internalized the distinction and live it out in every dimension of their lives.
verses.73:
> ˹They are˺ those who, when reminded of the revelation of their Lord, do not turn a blind eye or a deaf ear to it

**The Qur'an's Recurring Theme of Spiritual Deafness and Blindness**

The metaphor of spiritual deafness and blindness runs through the Qur'an. In 22:46 — "Truly it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind" — the Qur'an distinguishes between physical and spiritual sight. In 2:18 — "They are deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not return" — the disbelievers are described in the same terms. In 7:179 — "They have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear" — the description is extended. By contrast, those who bear the title of God's servants are the opposite of these descriptions: they hear, they see, they understand, and they return. The contrast between the servants and the disbelievers is the contrast between the open heart and the closed one, and the openness is the result of the humility, prayer, and repentance that define the servants' character.

These devoted servants have all three faculties: they hear the signs of God (25:73), they see the signs of God (25:61-62), and they speak the truth (25:72: they do not bear false witness).

**The Contrast With the Disbelievers' Response to Revelation**

The servants' receptivity to the signs stands in sharp contrast to the disbelievers' response described earlier in the sūrah. In 25:4-5, the disbelievers said: "This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but a fabrication... These are only fables of the ancients." In 25:21, they said: "We have never heard of this in any previous faith." In 25:30, the Prophet lamented: "My people have abandoned this Quran." The disbelievers heard the same signs that the servants heard, but they responded with rejection rather than receptivity. The difference is not in the signs but in the hearts: the servants' hearts were open, and the disbelievers' hearts were closed. The sūrah's placement of 25:73 after the description of the punishment (25:69) and the promise of forgiveness (25:70-71) suggests that the disbelievers' deafness and blindness are not permanent conditions but choices — choices that can be reversed through repentance and faith.

The word *ṣumman* (deaf) and *ʿumyānān* (blind) are used here in the accusative, functioning as adverbial descriptions of the manner in which the disbelievers fall upon the signs.
