The grammar itself tells a story: the deafness and blindness are not the servants' condition but the disbelievers' condition — the condition of those who refuse to hear and refuse to see. Those who stand in God's service have chosen the opposite condition: they hear with open ears and see with open eyes, and the openness is the foundation of their faith. The sūrah's contrast between the open and the closed is one of its most persistent themes, and 25:73 is the verse that states it most directly. The servants are open; the disbelievers are closed; and the difference between openness and closure is the difference between Paradise and Hell.
verses.74:
> ˹They are˺ those who pray, “Our Lord! Bless us with ˹pious˺ spouses and offspring who will be the joy of our hearts, and make us models for the righteous.”

**The Prayer for Family**

The verse records the servants' most personal prayer: *wa'lladhīna yaqūlūna Rabbanā hab lanā min azwājinā wa dhurriyyātinā qurrata aʿyunin* — "and those who say, 'Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring the coolness of our eyes.'" The word *qurrata aʿyunin* (coolness of the eyes) is an Arabic idiom for comfort, joy. The relief that comes from seeing something one loves. The servants do not pray for wealth, for status, or for worldly power. They pray for their families — for spouses and children who will be a source of joy and spiritual comfort. The prayer reveals the servants' priorities: the most important thing in their lives is not what they have but who they share their lives with. The quality they seek in their companions is spiritual — not beauty, not wealth, but the "coolness of the eyes" that comes from shared faith and mutual devotion.

Al-Rāzī observes that the "coolness of the eyes" is understood to be of a spiritual nature, not mere worldly enjoyment. The servants pray that their families will join them in worship and obedience — that the spouse will be a partner in faith and the children will be a continuation of the tradition. The Qur'an elsewhere warns against treating family as a distraction from God: "Your wealth and your children are only a trial" (64:15). The servants' prayer resolves the tension: they ask not that their families be a source of worldly comfort but that they be a source of spiritual comfort — the comfort of shared devotion, of a household oriented toward God.

**The Prayer for Leadership**

Al-Rāzī connects this prayer to Abraham's prayer in 26:84 — "And grant me a reputation of honor among later generations" — and notes that the desire for spiritual leadership is a positive thing when it comes from a desire to serve rather than to dominate. The servants of the Compassionate want to be models for the righteous — not because they seek status but because they want their lives to be useful, to be a guide for others who are trying to find the Way (*sabīl*).

**The Verse's Place in the Servants' Portrait**

The contrast between the servants' aspiration and the disbelievers' ambition could not be sharper. In 25:8, the disbelievers said: "Why was this ˹Quran˺ not sent down to some great man from the two cities?" — revealing their obsession with worldly status. The servants of the Compassionate do not pray for the kind of greatness the disbelievers admire; they pray for the kind of greatness that comes from serving God and serving the community. The difference is the difference between the two worldviews the sūrah has been presenting: the worldview that measures value by wealth and power, and the worldview that measures value by faith and service. The servants have chosen the latter, and the prayer of 25:74 is the expression of that choice.
verses.75:
> It is they who will be rewarded with ˹elevated˺ mansions ˹in Paradise˺ for their perseverance, and will be received with salutations and ˹greetings of˺ peace

**The Reward for Patience**

The verse describes the reward that awaits the servants of the Compassionate: *ulā'ika yujzawna'l-ghurfata bi-mā ṣabarū* — "Those are the ones who will be rewarded with the elevated chamber for their patience." The word *ghurfah* (elevated chamber, lofty abode) refers to the highest rooms of Paradise — the apartments closest to God's presence, the most honored positions in the Hereafter. The servants' patience was showed in every aspect of their lives: patience with the foolish (25:63), patience in night prayer (25:64), patience in spending (25:67), patience in avoiding sin (25:68), and patience in the face of a society that mocked and rejected them.

The word *ghurfah* appears in 29:58 — "And those who believed and did righteous deeds, We will surely give them lofty chambers in Paradise, beneath which rivers flow" — and in 34:37 — "And it is not your wealth or your children that bring you nearer to Us in station. It is whoever believes and does righteous deeds; for them there will be a double reward for what they did. They will be in lofty chambers, secure." The repetition across the Qur'an establishes the *ghurfah* as the highest reward in Paradise — not merely a dwelling but a position, a station, a level of closeness to God that surpasses everything else.

**The Verses of Reward as Counterbalance to the Verses of Punishment**

The reward described in 25:75 mirrors the punishment described in 25:69 in precise detail. In 25:69, the punishment is multiplied; in 25:75, the reward is a mansion. In 25:69, the condemned abide forever; in 25:76, the servants abide forever. In 25:69, the condemned are in disgrace; in 25:75, the servants are greeted with peace. The symmetry is the sūrah's way of presenting the two outcomes as mirror images: the same structure, the same language, the same permanence — and opposite qualities. The sūrah does not need to argue for the justice of the two outcomes; it shows them, and the showing is the argument.

The concept of *ṣabr* (patience, perseverance) as the basis for the reward is significant. The servants are not rewarded for their wealth, their status, their lineage, or their intelligence. They are rewarded for their patience — the quality that sustained them through every trial the sūrah described. The patience of walking humbly (25:63) in a world that rewards arrogance. The patience of praying at night (25:64) in a world that values sleep. The patience of spending moderately (25:67) in a world that worships excess. The patience of avoiding sin (25:68) in a world that normalizes transgression. The patience of passing by falsehood (25:72) in a world that celebrates it. Every act of patience was an act of resistance — resistance against the disbelievers' culture, against the pressure to conform, against the temptation to take the easy path. The reward for resistance is the *ghurfah*, and the *ghurfah* is the proof that the resistance was worth it.

The greeting is not from other human beings alone but from God Himself, as 36:58 confirms: "Peace! — a word from a Merciful Lord." The *salām* the servants receive in Paradise is the ultimate expression of divine approval: God greets them with the same word they used to greet the world.
verses.76:
> staying there forever. What an excellent place to settle and reside

**The Echo of 25:66**

The verse closes with *niʿma mustaqarran wa muqāmān* — "What an excellent settlement and abode!" The phrase uses the same two words — *mustaqarr* (settlement) and *muqām* (abode) — that appeared in 25:66, where the servants described Hell as "an evil place to settle and reside." The verbal echo is the sūrah's final structural device: the same vocabulary describes both outcomes, and the only difference is the adjective. In 25:66, the word was *sā'at* (evil); in 25:76, the word is *niʿma* (excellent, blessed). The contrast is the sūrah's way of presenting the two options in their starkest form: the same words, the same structure, the same finality — and opposite results. The choice between the two is the choice the sūrah has been offering since its first verse, and the servants of the Compassionate are the people who chose correctly.

The word *niʿma* (excellent, blessed) is the Qur'anic standard for the highest praise. It appears in 16:30 — "What an excellent servant! He was truly one who turned in repentance" — and in many other verses where God praises those who obey. Its use in 25:76 is God's own assessment of the servants' dwelling: not merely good, not merely pleasant, but *niʿma* — excellent, blessed, the best that can be. The servants' dwelling in Paradise is the highest form of existence, and the description of it as *niʿma* is the sūrah's final word on the subject.

**The Completion of the Servants' Portrait**

Verse 25:76 completes the portrait of the servants that began in 25:63. Across fourteen verses, the sūrah has described the servants' humility (25:63), their night prayer (25:64), their fear of Hell (25:65-66), their moderation (25:67), their moral boundaries (25:68), their rejection of falsehood (25:72), their receptivity to revelation (25:73), and their personal aspirations (25:74). The portrait is the sūrah's answer to the question posed in 25:1: what does the Criterion produce? The answer is: the servants of the Compassionate. The Criterion (25:1) was sent down to distinguish truth from falsehood, and the servants are the living embodiment of the distinction. They are the people who accepted the Criterion, lived by it, and were rewarded for it with the highest chambers of Paradise. The portrait is the sūrah's most sustained argument for the value of faith: not a philosophical proof but a description of what faith looks like when it is lived.

**The Structural Position of 25:76 in the Sūrah**

Verse 25:76 is the last verse of the servants' portrait and the penultimate verse of the sūrah. Its position is strategic: the portrait ends with the reward (25:75-76), not with the description of the servants' daily conduct (25:63-74). The sūrah's final message about the servants is therefore not about what they do but about what they receive — not about the effort but about the result. The result is the *ghurfah* (elevated chamber), the *salām* (peace), the *khālidīn* (eternal abiding), and the *niʿma* (excellence). The result is the answer to every act of patience, every night of prayer, every walk of humility, and every word of peace. The sūrah's portrait of the servants is therefore not only a description but a promise: the promise that the servants' lives — lived in accordance with the Criterion — will be rewarded with the best that God has to offer, and the reward will last forever.

The word *muqāmān* (abode, dwelling) in 25:76, compared with *maqīl* (resting place) in 25:24, reveals a subtle difference in the sūrah's vocabulary of Paradise. The permanence of the *muqām* is the opposite of the transience of earthly life: in this world, every dwelling is temporary — the house will crumble, the city will decay, the earth itself will pass away.

The servants who persevered (25:75) will remain in their elevated chambers forever; the condemned who violated the prohibitions (25:68-69) will remain in their disgrace forever.
verses.77:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “You ˹all˺ would not ˹even˺ matter to my Lord were it not for your faith ˹in Him˺. But now you ˹disbelievers˺ have denied ˹the truth˺, so the torment is bound to come.”

**The Inevitability of the Torment**

The verse's closing clause — *fa-qad waqa'a'l-wa'd* — "so the torment is bound to come" or "so the promise has fallen" — declares the inevitability of the consequence. The word *waqa'a* (to fall, to happen, to occur) uses the past tense, giving the punishment the quality of something that has already happened — not a future possibility but a settled fact. The promise of punishment is as certain as the promise of reward, and the certainty is the sūrah's final message to the disbelievers: the time for argument is over, the time for mockery has passed, and what remains is the consequence. The word *wa'd* (promise) applies to both reward and punishment in the Qur'an — God's promise to the righteous is Paradise, and His promise to the disbelievers is the fire.

**The Sūrah's Architecture**

Verse 25:77 closes the circle that opened in 25:1. The sūrah began with *tabāraka* — "Blessed is the One Who sent down the Criterion" — and it ends with the Prophet commanded to speak the final word to the disbelievers. Between the opening and the closing, the sūrah has presented the disbelievers' objections (25:4-8, 25:21), the Last-Day consequences (25:11-19, 25:22-29), the Prophet's consolation (25:30-31), the explanation of gradual revelation (25:32-33), the prophetic catalogue (25:35-40), the second cycle of mockery (25:41-44), the natural signs (25:45-55), the definition of the prophetic mission (25:56-60), the cosmic signs (25:61-62). The portrait of the servants of the Compassionate (25:63-76). The sūrah's structure is comprehensive: it addresses every possible objection, presents every possible form of evidence, and offers every possible incentive for faith. The final verse is the sūrah's last word: the disbelievers have been given everything they need, and the consequence of their refusal is now inevitable. The Criterion has been sent down; the servants have been described; the choice has been presented; and the choice is theirs.

The sūrah's final word — *fa-qad waqa'a'l-wa'd* ("so the torment is bound to come") — is also a reassurance for the Prophet and his followers. The disbelievers' mockery, their wealth, their social power — none of it will protect them from the consequence of their disbelief. The Prophet, who endured their mockery with patience (25:63: the servants say peace to the foolish), can take comfort in the certainty of the promise: the torment will come, the justice will be served, and the truth will prevail. The sūrah's final word is therefore not only a warning to the disbelievers but a consolation to the believers — a promise that the world's injustices will be corrected, that the mockers will be punished, and that the servants of the Compassionate will be rewarded. The Criterion has been sent down, and the Criterion will have the last word.
